speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Goods and Services Tax (Amendment) Bill 2022 covers six amendments.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Two give effect to measures that were announced in my Budget Statement this year.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The other four arise from our periodic review of the GST regime to clarify tax rules and to improve administration.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: MOF had sought views from the public on the draft Bill in June.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We published our responses to the key feedback received on 10 October 2022.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We thank the contributors for their inputs and have incorporated their suggestions where relevant.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clause 4 of the amendments will give effect to this change.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The proposed change in our GST rate has been robustly debated in this House but let me reiterate a few points.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have been expanding support for their needs, including their healthcare, social and ageing needs, and we will continue to do more.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We also want to improve social mobility, invest in skills upgrading and green our economy and city.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To achieve all this, we will need more Government spending – on a structural and recurring basis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is why at this year’s Budget, I had raised a slate of taxes, including Personal Income Tax, Property Tax, GST and the ARF rates for vehicles.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is how, as a responsible Government, we plan ahead and we meet our future needs in a sustainable way.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This GST rate increase is an important revenue move that will provide us with additional resources to meet our growing healthcare expenditures and to take better care of our growing number of seniors.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Government will help all Singaporeans adjust to the GST increase, especially the less well-off.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will help every Singaporean family through the Assurance Package.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We had already planned for this at the same time as we planned for the GST rate increase.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Members will know that at Budget 2020, Deputy Prime Minister Heng and then-Finance Minister set aside $6 billion for the Assurance Package.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Put another way, they will effectively not face additional GST expenses for many years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we will continue to uphold these commitments even as the inflationary outlook evolves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In my Budget Statement, I gave an example of a middle-income family of four with two school-going children, living in a 4-room flat and earning a monthly household income of around $8,000.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At that time, we estimated that they will incur GST on household expenses of around $3,400 a month, or $40,000 a year.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With a two percentage-point increase in GST, this means their additional GST expenses would amount to around $800 per year.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Under the Assurance Package, the family would have received around $4,000 in benefits.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, $4,000 in benefits, compared to $800 in additional expenses per year, that is about five times, which means that the Government pays about five years’ worth of the family’s additional GST.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That was the computation we made earlier this year in the Budget.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With higher inflation this year and in the coming years, we can expect that the household expenditure and therefore the additional GST expenses will increase.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I will share the details of this enhancement in my Budget Statement next year.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, for those who ask the Government to delay the GST rate increase, the Assurance Package in effect does precisely that, for the majority of households.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The cash and other forms of support under the Assurance Package amount to more than what most citizens will pay in additional GST for at least five years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I have explained how the Assurance Package works and how it is for all Singaporean households and provides a cushion to ease the transition.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because people say the Assurance Package, no matter how generous is temporary.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Yes, but they do not fully understand that there is also another important design feature of GST which is a permanent GSTV scheme and the absorption of GST for subsidised education and healthcare.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Households already receive these offsets today and as permanent measures, they will continue alongside, and even after, the Assurance Package.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Through the GSTV, we help lower- to middle-income households defray a significant part of their GST expenses permanently.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The GSTV scheme has four components: cash; MediSave for seniors to support their medical needs; U-Save rebates to offset utilities bills; and S&CC rebates to offset S&CC bills.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Besides the GSTV, we will continue to absorb GST for publicly subsidised healthcare and education.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, after putting together the permanent GSTV and GST absorption – what we have is an overall GST system that taxes consumption in a fair and effective manner.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: What are some of our features of our system?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In effect, we have a multi-tiered GST system – one that is tiered by income levels, with lower-income households paying a much lower effective GST rate than higher-income households.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That means the GST increase will not negatively impact them.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The full impact of the GST will be borne largely by higher-income households, as well as tourists and foreigners who are based here – and this is also the group that contributes the biggest share to net GST revenues from households and individuals.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And as the inflationary outlook evolves, we will continue to monitor our scheme parameters to ensure that we uphold and maintain these objectives.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The GST is therefore a key part of our fair and progressive system of taxes and transfers that takes care of the less well-off and ensures that those who are better off contribute their fair share in revenues.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The second amendment updates the GST treatment for a supply of travel arranging services.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Examples of such services include the arranging and facilitation of international transport, accommodation and travel insurance.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, the basis for determining whether a supply of travel arranging services is zero-rated or standard-rated depends on factors like the location of the accommodation or whether the transportation being arranged is international in nature.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, for the arranging of accommodation, if the accommodation is located in Singapore, today GST applies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But if the accommodation is located abroad, then the supply of arranging the accommodation today is zero-rated, which means that it is not subject to GST.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But today's treatment does not accurately reflect the place of consumption of such travel arranging services.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Such arranging or facilitation services are in fact consumed by the Singapore-based consumer at the point of booking, rather than at the eventual place of consumption of the underlying travel product.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are therefore updating the GST treatment of travel arranging services under clause 7 and with effect from 1 January 2023, the GST treatment for a supply of travel arranging services will be based on where the person who contracts for the service and where the person who directly benefits from the service belong.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, if the contractual customer of the service belongs in Singapore, then GST will be charged at the standard rate.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This amendment will also ensure consistent GST treatment for travel arranging services, regardless of whether they are rendered by local or overseas providers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Today, overseas providers of travel arranging services already have to charge GST when providing services to Singapore-based customers, irrespective of where the underlying travel product such as accommodation is.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 8, 12, 13, 14 and 15 update the Transitional Rules in the GST Act.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These Rules are to be applied during a change in GST rate or treatment.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Based on the Rules, taxpayers will determine whether the old or new GST rate or treatment applies to their supplies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The amendments provide greater clarity in the application of the rules, particularly for more unique supplies made, such as supplies which spans both a change in GST rate and the effective date of GST registration of a business.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Next, clauses 2, 3, 5, 16, 17, 19 and 20 refine the rules for taxing low-value goods and imported services under the Overseas Vendor Registration (OVR) and Reverse Charge (RC) regimes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The refinements seek to prevent double taxation, provide tax certainty, and ease the compliance burden of businesses.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, to prevent double taxation, the refinements clarify that where overseas vendors procure services already charged with GST from Singapore suppliers and subsequently onward supply these same services to their own customers in Singapore, they need not charge GST on these onward supplies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is provided the overseas vendors are on the “pay-only” regime where they do not make any claims for refund of GST they incur on their purchases.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The next amendment relates to our efforts to counter Missing Trader Fraud.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Missing Trader Fraud is a fraud scheme used by syndicates, where the seller absconds with the GST he has collected on his sales without paying the GST to IRAS, while businesses further down the fraud chain continue to claim refunds from IRAS on input GST paid on their purchases.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In 2020, we introduced several measures to deter Missing Trader Fraud schemes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This included denying input GST refund claims to businesses who knew or should have known that their purchases were part of a fraudulent arrangement, as well as introducing a 10% surcharge to be applied on the amount of input GST denied.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These measures targeted businesses that did not conduct the appropriate due diligence when entering into business arrangements.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To directly target the perpetrators of Missing Trader Fraud, criminal sanctions based on a two-tiered approach are now proposed to be introduced from 1 January 2023.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Tier 1 offences apply to Missing Trader Fraud masterminds, co-conspirators and syndicate members who participate in such fraud schemes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The proposed sanctions are proportionate to the severity of the offences and are aligned with the sanctions for similar offences under other Acts, like the Penal Code and Companies Act.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 6, 10, 11, and 18 of the Bill provide for this amendment.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A similar amendment was earlier passed under the Income Tax (Amendment) Bill 2022, to empower the Comptroller to extend all filing deadlines in the Income Tax Act as well as the Property Tax Act.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These changes will put us in a better position to fund our common aspirations and to build a fairer and more inclusive Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The effects of the war in Ukraine and the never-ending pandemic have led to rising energy and food prices among others, which are now being felt at all households and businesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singaporeans are feeling the strain, with many households’ essential items like electricity bills, groceries at the supermarket, food at the hawker centre and coffee shops rising sharply.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The low- to middle-income and the retirees are particularly impacted as they do not have the higher wages or savings to offset the cost increases.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, the question then is whether should we go ahead with the GST increase at the current time?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: To answer this question, we need to go back to the fundamentals.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Why do we need to raise the GST in the first place?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government has explained that our expenditures are rising and in the decades ahead, we will need to spend even more.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our population is rapidly ageing and along with it comes rising healthcare needs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I have seen that first-hand in my constituency Bukit Panjang, where the demand for healthcare and senior care facilities has risen.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have recently opened a polyclinic in our town and it has been full house since day one of opening.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There are increasing demand for places, for more senior care centres, dialysis centres and rehabilitation centres – there are always queues waiting – which we intend to further expand our capacity in coming years.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: If we postpone them, then we will not be doing right for our seniors, who could be our parents and grandparents of today and the future.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Besides ageing and healthcare-related spending, we would also need more funding for capacity building, climate mitigation, energy resilience, security, education, childcare and the various social and employment support that we want to do more of.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, there is no dispute on the need for higher spending and hence, the need for higher revenue to fund these escalating expenditures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government believes that a major bulk of our recurrent expenditures should be funded by recurrent revenues so that our fiscal finances are on a sustainable footing.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Property taxes, which tend to be cyclically driven, is expected to contribute about $2 billion in FY2022/23.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government does review our tax rates from time to time and adjust them as appropriate.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In recent years, due to higher funding needs, the Government has indeed been raising tax rates.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In Budget 2022, income tax and wealth taxes, including property and vehicle taxes were raised.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government has also increased the stamp duties and the ABSDs, which is another form of wealth tax, besides using it as a tool to cool the market.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is the Government's approach, which is to build a diversified stream of revenues that is stable and sustainable to pay for our current and longer-term spending commitments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: GST is one stream of revenue that adds to the diversification, where in our unique system, we actually take in more taxes from the wealthier groups through GST – those with higher purchasing power – and at the same time, mitigate the impact to the lower-income or no-income Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Workers' Party disagrees, saying that current cost of living and inflation is high so we should not add further to the costs; that GST is regressive and it hurts the middle and low-income; and that there are alternative sources of revenue.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In their recent Hammer article, they said there are four alternatives to raising GST: (a) raise NIRC from 50% to 60%; (b) to use a portion of land sales for recurrent expenditure and raise property taxes for more expensive properties; (c) to increase corporate tax revenue from the compliance with BEPS 2; and (d) raise other taxes like carbon tax and sin taxes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the article, they even said that the amount we can get from any of these four, will produce the same amount of revenue annually as a 2% GST increase.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Therefore, just do any one of these and there is no need to raise GST.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Looking at the previous debates and what the Government has been doing, this is what I see.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government understands that the GST will add to costs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But at the same time, the Government would have to make sure that we have the stable base of revenues that can cover our long-term recurring expenditures, especially healthcare, as our population ages rapidly over the next few years.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, the Government's strategy is to strengthen our revenue sources, which also includes increasing the GST rate, but balance this with a two-pronged approach to cushion the middle income, the low-income and the retirees against both cost of living and the GST increase.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For cost of living, there are support packages.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Earlier in the year, Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said that if there was a need to do more, the Government would do more.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There was an additional $1.5 billion package in June.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, there is a total of $3.5 billion of targeted support.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There is also the Enhanced Permanent GST vouchers, separate from the Assurance Package, with additional cash payouts.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Separately, the Government will also absorb the additional GST on publicly funded healthcare and education.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The GST offset support has been in existence for about 15 years.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It has very much been a permanent feature in our GST system to help neutralise the impact of GST to lower-income Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The offsets focus rightly on essentials like utilities, S&CC, MediSave and a cash component as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: On the ground, I have seen these being very helpful to reduce the cost impact of GST to low- to middle-income Singaporeans, especially to the seniors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is the uniqueness of our GST system, where the lower-income groups have largely been cushioned, while we raise a larger proportion of the GST from the higher spending group, which tends to be the wealthier, the high-income and also includes the foreign visitors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These two approaches are designed to cushion the middle-income, the lower-income and the retirees against both cost of living and the GST increase.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This tells us we can be assured of support to get through this tough time and that those who need more help will get more.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: At the same time, we can also be assured that when we get older, we will also get healthcare and other support because we will have a diversified and more stable source of revenues to pay for our various spending programmes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: What about the Workers' Party’s four alternative sources?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I believe these were debated in the Budget debate earlier this year.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I found Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong’s round-up speech very helpful in understanding why there are reservations and doubts about the Workers' Party’s proposals.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: What that means basically is that we will put back less into the reserves.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It also means less for our young people when they get older.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This would reduce the NIRC that we can generate for subsequent years, including next year, and the cumulative impact over time will be even more significant.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our NIRC has grown from $7.6 billion in 2012 to $21.5 billion this year, based on Budget 2022 estimates.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We hope that NIRC can continue contribute more, not by changing the ratio but by growing this base amount of our reserves.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: If we have not saved enough in the past, the NIRC today would be even lower and we would end up needing higher taxes or we may have to cut spending and subsidies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Surely, we want this NIRC annuities to keep growing to fund more spending and to reduce future tax burden for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Workers' Party also mentioned about land sales which was earlier dealt with in the earlier Parliamentary Questions, both answered by Minister Indranee.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I will not talk about that, except to just mention about the property tax that the Workers' Party mentioned for the expensive properties.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government has already made some moves this year, in this year's Budget for the non-owner-occupied residential properties.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It was raised from 10% to 20% range to 12% to 36% range.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But the point is whether raising property tax from just the high-end properties would be enough – unless we raise it so high that it is untenable.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: If want to keep it tenable, then we may have to increase the taxes on other owner-occupied properties – which will impact the middle-income households and HDB owners.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Do not get me wrong, we are not in a disagreement about increasing property taxes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: That can be another source, but the question is at what rate and how much can you raise it to?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: On corporate tax, it was also mentioned that there will be increased corporate tax revenue due to the BEPS Pillar Two.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: At this point in time, there is no visibility on the actual figures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: More importantly, it does not take into account the potential outflows from BEPS, as there is a Pillar One and Pillar Two.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There is no certainty that the revenue from BEPS Pillar Two will be as what the Workers' Party had produced in their calculations, as we cannot assume that companies will not shift their operations in response to the tax rate increases.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Having said that, I do not disagree that corporate tax should be another source of additional revenue that the Government should tap on as we do need all the revenue that we can get to fund a long list of our future spending needs – like I said, the economic capabilities building, transport, childcare, unemployment support and others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We need more funding and, if corporate tax can be another source, why not?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The key balancing consideration is whether the increase in corporate tax rate will compromise our competitive position, which would have direct implications on jobs and other opportunities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: On carbon tax and sin taxes, we are already tapping on these sources and, in my view, there are more upsides.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: On carbon tax, the question is how high and how fast we can increase.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can the businesses withstand it and how much would be passed on consumers, especially when we know that a higher carbon tax could mean higher household electricity bills.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There is a carbon tax debate coming up and I look forward to hearing the Workers' Party's proposal on the carbon tax rate.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Perhaps, it is good to hear also how high we should raise the tobacco tax rate to, to make up for the 2% GST.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Being more prudent in our finances has never failed us in our history; it has strengthened us.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While we recognise that the GST hike is meant to meet growing expenditure needs, the Workers' Party has consistently made clear our view that the GST hike is not necessary and that there are ways to raise recurrent revenue without resorting to an increase in GST, especially against the backdrop of macroeconomic uncertainties and soaring inflation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The only responsible approach is not to proceed with the GST hike without seriously considering the other better alternatives to secure the revenues we need, which the Workers' Party has described in detail during the 2022 Budget Debates earlier this year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Before I touch on why I believe the GST hike is not at all appropriate, particularly given the current circumstances, I do recognise the sets of support packages provided to our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Given how our fiscal position has and is shaping up to be, it is, after all, the right thing to do.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first $1.5 billion package announced on 21 June provides relief for lower-income households and vulnerable groups.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The package will be funded from the better-than-expected fiscal outturn in FY2021.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I have shared in my Stamp Duty (Amendment) Bill speech in July this year, actual operating revenue collections for FY2021 turned out to be higher, compared to what was initially budgeted in Budget 2021 and even the revised estimates for Budget 2022 announced earlier this year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This would already be more than sufficient to cover the first $1.5 billion support package.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, both operating and development expenditures are lower by a combined $3.6 billion, which, I understand, is due to lower-than-budgeted spending on COVID-19 response measures as the Omicron variant turned out less severe than anticipated.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In September this year, I asked a Parliamentary Question on the current FY2022's to-date operating revenue, operating expenditure, development expenditure and the primary surplus deficit respectively and how these figures compare with the budgeted figures.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In his reply, Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong noted that it is generally not meaningful to compare the latest revenue and expenditure figures against the budgeted figures so early in the financial year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I was thus a bit surprised that just one month later, on 14 October, the Government announced a second $1.5 billion support package, which will be funded from better-than-expected fiscal outturn in the first half of FY2022.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Put another way, comparing revenue data on a year-on-year basis would suggest that operating revenues have cumulatively increased by 14% year-on-year or $5.8 billion in the first half of FY2022 alone.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This will compare favourably to the projected increase of $1.4 billion for the full year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even if we include the additional $1.5 billion package from October, there appears to be sufficient budgetary slack for the rest of the financial year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong may say that we cannot rely on sentiment-driven collections, such as like stamp duties, which can fluctuate from year to year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, the increase in revenues was driven by tax revenues led by corporate income tax at $3.5 billion, GST at around $900 million and personal income taxes at around $700 million.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Is it not fair for us to ask is there really a need to push through the GST hike so urgently, especially when the effects of inflation have also partially contributed to the almost $1 billion year-on-year increase in GST collections in just the first half of the year alone?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This brings me to my next point on inflation, where I still recall Minister of State Low Yen Ling's response to Parliamentary Questions in February this year where she shared then that MAS' core inflation is expected to increase in the first half of 2022 before easing in the latter part of the year for headline inflation to average 1.5% to 2.5% in 2022 and that both MTI and MAS do not expect persistent accelerating inflation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In its October monetary policy statement, MAS noted that core inflation is likely to stay around 5% for the rest of 2022 and remain high in the first half of 2023.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, MAS expects headline inflation to average 6% in 2022 and stay elevated at 5.5% to 6.5% in 2023.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I fully agree with MAS that there are upside risks to this inflation forecast, including second round effects associated with a prolonged period of high inflation, which the Deputy Prime Minister also warned that it is unlikely that we return to a period of low inflation during his press conference last month.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Do we really want to fan the flames of inflation and contribute an additional unnecessary one percentage point increase in the cost of living?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am not much of a football person but, when your team is 5-0 down, does it make sense to respond by scoring an own goal?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The key words I want to highlight is "this year".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Using MOF's illustration of a middle-income couple with two young children, the estimated annual household expenditure that incurs GST will amount to $40,320, which I assume to be based on average expenditure from 2018 to 2020.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What is even more worrying is that, as shared by Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, we must also be realistic that inflation is not going to go back to the situation where we were used to over the past decade where it was very low rates of inflation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even if inflation eases eventually, prices are not going to come down and will continue to increase, exacerbating cost of living pressures for our fellow Singaporean households.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My next point is then simply that Assurance Packages are temporary while a GST hike is forever.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recognise that the previously announced Assurance Package was supposed to offset about five years' worth of additional GST for most households.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With the effects of inflation coming in hard, these five years' worth of offset is looking to be increasingly diminished.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, I do recognise the $1.4 billion top-up to the Assurance Package, which the Deputy Prime Minister has just announced.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The blunting of the near-term impact from the GST hike from the Assurance Package is a welcome salve for low- to middle-income households.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But as we look forward into the horizon and take into context the very challenging road ahead, given the persistent inflationary environment, will low- to middle-income households then be on the hook for the higher GST rates after the benefits of the Assurance Package wear off, even after the topped-up Assurance Package?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Again, do we really want the successive GST hikes to be the straw that breaks the camel's back for our fellow Singaporeans who are already struggling with the cost of living?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Singapore's GDP growth will come in below trend in 2023 and downside risks have intensified.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Against a deteriorating macroeconomic backdrop with significant downside risks in the global and domestic economies, a GST hike at this point is counterintuitive and could lead to a lower path for GDP and private consumption.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There was no COVID-19, commodity prices were half of what they are today and inflation rates were one-tenth of what they are today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To summarise, the timing of the proposed GST hike could not be any worse and it is irresponsible to proceed with it.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is especially so, considering the fiscally viable alternatives which have not been given due consideration, soaring inflation driving up the cost of living significantly and the fact that assistance packages provided are only temporary versus the GST hike, which is forever.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, as the hon Member would know, this framework was created in, I believe, 2008 when the Government decided that as society changes, it is time to reset the balance between how much of those investment returns get rolled back into the reserves and how much actually goes into the Budget.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Given all the trends we have talked about, the ageing society, the fact that Government expenditures are going to go up and so on, I would like to ask Mr Liang on this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Does he not agree that this balance point should be reviewed from time to time as the needs for Government spending changes, or does he think that this 50% ceiling should be set in stone forever?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And if he agrees that it should be reviewed from time to time, when does he think should it be reviewed again?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: But, in my view, we have not come to the dire state where we have to make changes in response to those differences, bearing in mind that we want to continue to accumulate the reserves, so that we can reinvest them and you can get the returns benefits straight, the year after.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Looking at the expenditures that we are seeing – I mentioned a few, not just for healthcare but even some for the infrastructure, energy resilience and so on – the spending is just going to escalate.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: In Hokkien, they say: "jit lang jit pua, kamcheng buay sua" (一人一半, 感情不散).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: That is how we strike a balance between future and current generations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a global centre for investments, we must strive to maintain Singapore's track record of stable governance in a key distinguishing feature, which is farsighted planning.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Three million, or sometimes, $3 billion or $3 trillion question, for any elected responsible government, is how to balance government expenditure against revenues.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are more and more things that we would like the Government to spend on to improve the lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But no one likes the idea of raising taxes to finance that.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, this Bill, if passed, allows appropriate changes to be done in the run-up to the GST increase.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On that note, I turn to this GST Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In my Adjournment Motion last month, I spoke about the new normal of higher interest rates and higher costs on our Singaporean households.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is even before the proposed GST increase and, understandably, people are concerned.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, I note that the Government has been taking steps to address current costs of living, even before the GST hike kicks in.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, MAS made five moves to appreciate the Singapore dollar since October last year and mitigated imported inflation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Two off-cycle tightening moves in January and July this year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This was done early by MAS and has been effective in reducing the impact of inflation on our import-dependent economy and, in some way, defended Singaporeans' purchasing power.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong explained in July this year, the stronger dollar had helped us keep the increase in food prices to 3%, even though the global increase was 20.3%.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The increase in energy prices was 13.6% in Singapore from January to May 2022, whereas the global increase was around 27.5%.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I would like to take this opportunity to thank MAS and the team managing and formulating the Singaporean dollar policy for the pre-emptive calibrated moves much earlier in 2021, before moves by other central banks were made and before all the headline inflation concerns reared its head significantly in 2022.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am sure we can trust this Government to further add to that support if the economic situation continues to worsen.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Seeing the recent developments, would further support packages be targeted at all Singaporeans rather than just a smaller segment?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That is a question that I would like to ask Deputy Prime Minister Wong.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If not, will the Government consider raising the per capita income threshold for the definition of lower-income households, so that the broader base of Singaporeans can benefit?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Since it was first announced in 2018, I note that the Government has been adjusting to economic conditions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It did not proceed with the GST increase in the height of the pandemic years and it has also taken the decision to stagger the GST increase over two years, so that consumers and businesses have time to adjust.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In light of the dynamic nature of the economic environment, I would like to ask the Minister for Finance several questions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some have been asked by other Members before, but in light of the changing economic environment now, I want to ask and seek the Minister's views again.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, should we delay the increase in view of heightened inflation?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, whether a GST increase is the right fiscal stance as part of the macro policy mix now, given the risk of inflationary pressures remaining sticky for longer and a weakening global and domestic economy, possibly in 2023 – and you never know, maybe slightly beyond that?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, would we proceed if there is a sharp deterioration in conditions?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And fourth, can we delay the increase if our fiscal needs are not urgent?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If the answer is that we should still proceed with the GST increase, then it must be implemented carefully.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We cannot leave the more vulnerable Singaporeans behind.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am cognisant that not many countries talk so much about GST offsets to mitigate its effects as much as Singapore, I think, and way in advance.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am thankful that there had been several announcements previously in the previous Budgets to offset the impact of the GST increase.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In this regard and on the basis of the economic environment we are in, and the macro outlook we are facing, I hope that the Minister for Finance and the Deputy Prime Minister, can assure our lower-income and middle-income households as well, and in particular, the sandwich class segments in Singapore, that they will be buffered against the GST increase, even in this heightened inflationary environment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The GST Voucher (GSTV) scheme is one of the ways in which the Government helps to buffer the middle- and lower-income against GST increase.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I would like to seek some clarifications to ensure that the GSTV scheme is able to meet this objective well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some of my residents have inquired on the GSTV scheme during my recent launch of the cost-of-living assistance programme, or CLAP as we call it in Toa Payoh East, a ground-up initiative involving the tripartite partners of the local merchants, residents and Toa Payoh East CCC Community Development and Welfare Fund (CDWF).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is aimed to supplement additional help to lower- and middle-income families beyond the Government's COL transfers or payments, and GSTV, to cope with the daily expenses and boost the businesses of our heartland merchants and hawkers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, has the Government conducted regular reviews to assess the need to raise the per capita income threshold, such that more households can qualify for permanent GSTV?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, the annual value of home is a key factor in the eligibility criteria of eight programmes, such as GSTV and CHAS schemes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Has the recent boom in the property market led to any significant increases in the annual value of homes, to the extent of affecting their occupiers' eligibility of schemes, like GSTV?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In terms of administration, how many of those eligible have yet to sign up for GSTV and what are the avenues available to those who are less digitally inclined and unfamiliar with checking the eligibility through the e-service?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How many of those eligible last year were sent cheques that they did not encash?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, could the Ministry also share what measures have been taken to minimise such expenses over the years?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will the new GovCash initiative be implemented this year reduce such processing expenditure?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is not the same for personal income tax or property taxes, which will definitely hit Singaporeans, but not necessarily our foreigner friends.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With our recovering tourism numbers post-COVID-19, it makes the GST increase an even more attractive revenue option.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If not, may I ask if the Government will do so.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Speaking for myself, I did take a while to understand the various illustrations provided in the Explanatory Statement to the Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While the amendments are unlikely to impact our neighbourhood store owners who typically provide one-off goods and services, such guides would help some of our local SMEs who might not fully grasp the options available to them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I also remain concerned about businesses taking the opportunity to increase their prices, at a rate that goes beyond passing on their costs to their consumers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Taking an example we are all familiar with, the prices of cooked food at our hawker centres and coffee shops, are usually hiked at 50 cents to $1 at a time, which is a substantial percentage increase where their base prices are around, on average, $4 today.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Any unjustified increases might not be high enough to pass the threshold to be reported to the Committee Against Profiteering; and even if they do, the average consumer is hardly going to report the economy rice or nasi padang stall for a higher price than they expected.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I would like to invite the Ministry or the Committee Against Profiteering to devise a systematic way to analyse costs increases on the ground, especially repeated increases in a short period of time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On the new measures in the bill to address missing trader fraud, can the Ministry also clarify what is the difference between the new section 62C, and the existing regime?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I understand that this is to catch a situation where a seller collects output GST on goods sold but disappears without paying it to the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the meantime, other parties in the supply chain continue to deduct input GST claims on purchases they have made.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The products are then exported by the last seller in the chain, who also does not need to pay GST to IRAS, since export sales are zero-rated.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If so, will the sentencing precedence under the existing regime still be applicable to guide the appropriate sentences under this new enhanced framework.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Workers' Party has opposed this increase and continues to do so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Nevertheless, in the spirit of advancing the debate, we have offered a number of, what we believe, are credible alternatives to the decision to stubbornly plough ahead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I previously shared with this House about why raising the GST is not ideal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To reiterate, perhaps ad nauseam, I spoke during the Budget debate about why raising GST was unnecessary, given alternative revenue options available.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I followed it up in an Adjournment Motion about how fiscal policy should not undermine our efforts at tackling inflation by increasing the headwinds that the economy faces.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More recently, I explained in my speech on the Income Tax (Amendment) Bill, why a temporary postponement of the GST hike – whilst clearly second best to not doing anything at all – would nevertheless allow the Government to better fulfil its promise of addressing inflation that was higher and more persistent than expected.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Now, you would think that I would have nothing else to add to this topic of GST and yet I do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While this is in our view, unambiguously inferior to some of the alternative revenue generation strategies that the Workers' Party has previously advocated, it may offer an important stop-gap measure that affords precious relief to our people at this time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, the Government's decision to implement the GST increase in an incremental fashion rather than in one fell swoop has been welcome by both businesses as well as many Members of this House.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, it is notable that even back in February, some consumers remained skeptical and this sentiment has probably been further compounded by the continued erosion of purchasing power in recent months due to stubbornly persistent inflation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is a strong likelihood that increase in GST will further feed this inflation monster.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In principle, this need not be the case.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Tax increases could well dampen overall demand and thereby tame rising prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But if taxes end up raising the costs faced by firms, they could instead, end up constricting supply and then give rise to price increases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In practice, we have often observed increases in the inflation following the introduction of Value Added Taxes, such as the GST.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The example I had previously shared with this House, the case of Japan, is instructive here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Japan increased its version of the GST thrice over the past quarter century.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Now, imagine a doubling of our inflation rate from our current already unbearable levels.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Now, to be completely fair, it should be noted that Japan's hikes occurred in a much more benign inflationary environment, which could have amplified the effects of the GST hike on inflation outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is nevertheless, difficult to envision conditions where the impending GST increase would not give rise to another bout of inflation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be fair, the Government has tried to get ahead of this possibility by convening the Commitee Against Profiteering.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This Committee is tasked with investigating feedback on unjustified price increases in essential items while using the GST hike as a cover.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet the task in front of the Commitee to effectively adjudicate cases of profiteering when the global inflation environment has itself ran amok, seems nigh well impossible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, how can we reasonably expect the Commitee to successfully disentangle the share of the price increase that is attributable to profiteering from a 1% GST hike when inflation itself is already running at more than seven times that rate?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong has explained that the Government believes that it is, and I quote, "more responsible", to proceed with the GST increase even amid the uncertain inflation outlook.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Inflation has hit the hardest in the categories that are often excluded from the so-called core measure of inflation commonly targeted by central banks, which is food and fuel.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, these selfsame goods and services are, not coincidentally, also frequently the most visible ones to the average consumer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the MAS officially targets a different definition of core, which excludes private transport and accommodation instead, these categories have, likewise, been among those that have experienced the greatest bouts of price increases in recent times.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Food prices overall have risen by 6.9% compared to a year ago.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But in certain categories, this increase is more stark and significantly greater than overall food inflation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The prices of fish, for instance, have jumped by an average of more than 10%, prompting another Member of this House, Mr Melvin Yong, to fret that if this trend of existing expensive fish will continue into the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It also makes it harder for the wallets of those of us who are trying to heed the call of Healthy SG to improve our diets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another Hokkien saying says "boh he, heh ma hoh", literally "no fish, prawns are good too".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, in April the price of prawns jumped by a whopping 14%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This has led to shock and dismay among others, my Sengkang residents, some of whom have come to us during Meet-the-People Sessions to ask for relief from overdue utilities bills, which they are finding difficulty in paying.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The culprit of high utilities prices is unsurprisingly, the high cost of energy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: High fuel prices have also reared their head in transport costs, which have increased by around a-fifth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We can, of course, lay the blame on the feet of the Russo-Ukrainian War.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the fact is that many are facing sticker shock when they book a Grab or a Gojek because they are late for an important business meeting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, while Singaporeans accept the inflation is very much a global phenomenon, the reality is that inflation has inadvertently become a tax on our people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government has tried to assuage some of this pain arising from this inflation tax with a range of incidental measures, such as issuing additional U-Save rebates, S&CC credits and CDC vouchers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The prices of public transport options have also been mostly kept in check.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such additional support, to be clear, helps, but, and especially for lower-income Singaporeans, including those that reside in Sengkang, appreciate this relief.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, those patches appear piecemeal and inadequate since they refer – they cater to the average household within each income group.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In our walkabouts, incredulous residents have come up to me and asked, "How can inflation be only 7% when my "cai peng" has doubled – has gone from $3 to $5, and my SP bill has doubled?" Herein lies the conundrum.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And so those who consume a narrower basket of goods and services will feel the pinch more acutely.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This leaves many individuals and families feeling like the coupons, subsidies and rebates fail to make up for the magnitude of the price increases that they face.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Their worries are compounded since by definition, spending on such necessities is seldom view as optional.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Since these categories have been subject to the greatest price volatility in recent months and given the enormous pocket share that such items command in the average household's budget, it is reasonable to offer temporary, targeted and relief for these essentially non-discretionary aspects of their spending.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My Sengkang colleague, Ms He Ting Ru, has previously made this case during her speech, during the annual Budget debates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This Government has counted that such a multi-rate GST system will benefit higher-income households more than low-income ones, making exemptions regressive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is, by and large true, although under normal economic circumstances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But we are not in a normal economic environment, are we?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Inflation is a generalised rise in prices and affects us all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: GST vouchers and U-Save rebates targeted to the lowest two or three quintiles of our economy leaves our large and beleaguered middle class in the lurch.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Recall, taxes paid by such households will tend to be nominally higher, assuming that they were lucky enough to receive a salary adjustment this year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, they would have been left without most of the additional support measures that have been targeted at the lower-income groups.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This then amounts to a real tax increase even before the GST hike.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, as Ms He has also pointed out, even if a system of exemptions turns out to be regressive, keeping the existing system of no exemptions may be even more regressive, since the pernicious effects of GST on the incomes of the poor may well be greater than the benefits of raising more revenue from the rich.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The other common argument is that multiple rates will complicate our system, raising compliance costs for businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But surely the current patchwork of credits, vouchers, rebates and subsidies is even more complicated to administer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, Ms He also stressed that modern technology essentially means that only a few additional lines of code are required to ensure that scan barcodes apply differentiated rates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Surely, our revenue collection systems are at least as sophisticated as those in advanced economies such as Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States, all of which along with emerging economies such as India, Indonesia and South Korea, employ some form of differentiated GST regime, and compliance is after all, limited to only the largest firms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my earlier speeches, I had explained how short-term macroeconomic conditions warranted continued support from easy fiscal policy, of which a postponement of the GST increase would be a form.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Today, I wish to also touch on how longer-term structural changes likewise lend credence to the notion of a temporary delay.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But those were extraordinary expenditures which were funded in part from our reserves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, if we now allow the rate of growth of healthcare expenditures to revert to its original trajectory of a steady 0.1% increase annually, we still have wiggle room to forestall an immediate increase in GST.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It strikes me that a postponement of GST for essential items will not have any significant detrimental effects on our fiscal balances and can eventually be made up in the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, a delay will make a substantial difference to families who are bearing the brunt of expensive necessities, today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, such a move would provide relief for even families not covered by the GST Voucher Scheme who nevertheless face the same price increases that we all do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: MOF has either not conducted studies of such a possibility, or if the Ministry has indeed performed such analysis, it has ever never disclosed its evaluations publicly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A temporary postponement of GST for selected basic necessities will offer a pilot that would allow the MOF to recover some real-time numbers for how the differentiated GST regime would operate in practice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is in the spirit of the usual approach that this Government adopts: to pragmatically test options that present themselves, to determine if it is a policy that is worth adopting and to calibrate the scope of the policy accordingly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I see I have a little bit of time yet, so I will just touch on a few points in rebuttal to arguments made about why some of the revenue options that we suggested are not quite tenable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One argument has been made is that property taxation would not raise quite enough for the purposes of offsetting the needed increase in GST amounts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The crux of where we think we can raise an additional amount comes from property sales.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Just to be clear – the way that we compute property sales does not suggest that we are taking non-recurrent permanent revenues and using it for recurring purposes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Likewise, on the issue of corporate taxation, it is important to note that our proposal of respecting the terms of the OECD BEPS agreement, essentially just operationalises what would be necessary to an agreement for which we are already a signatory.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In fact, we will not touch SMEs and our estimates of a net revenue increase are not ours alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Others such as Mr See, who wrote in The Straits Times in 28 February, pointed out how BEPS was unlikely to hurt competitiveness and may net Singapore net gains in revenue as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Would our proposal of going from 50% to 60% necessarily mean that we are still under-saving or are we over-saving?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I think these should all be kept in mind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While some may cope better than others, higher prices affect everybody: businesses and consumers, rich and poor.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Raising the GST is more than likely to exacerbate these inflation pressures that our citizens already face.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I should point out, however, that there is one entity that is comparatively shielded from this rise in inflation: the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That is because many taxes are collected as a percentage of the taxable base.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For example, if a business raises prices in response to higher costs of raw materials, it will earn more revenue in dollar terms, and hence, its greater nominal profits will now be subject to corporate taxes, even if the tax rate remains completely unchanged.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Let us not shackle Singaporeans with yet another chain around their ankles when there are alternative ways forward.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Workers and unions are concerned the rising cost of living and the need to adapt to new ways of working.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But their primary concern has always been: “Can their wages keep up with rising costs of living?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Would the increase in GST worsen the cost-of-living problems?” The anxieties are real and lived, but workers also keenly understand that higher costs are here to stay and longer-term solutions are needed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The time-tested solution is a three-pronged one: firstly, timely assistance during exigencies; two, sustainable wage growth in the long term; and three, moderating costs of living.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This was in addition to the $1.5 billion that was given out in June 2022.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These short-term packages help to blunt the impact of sharp increases in costs during unprecedented inflation globally.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Workers are assured that if inflation remains high, Government will continue to support them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: My fellow Labour Member of Parliament, Ms Yeo Wan Ling, will share how these packages have helped our lower-wage and our self-employed workers to cope.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The lasting solution is we must keep wages growing ahead of inflation sustainably.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We appreciate that costs of doing business have increased.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Singapore is a price-taker for virtually any items we import.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are price-takers for most of our factors of production.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Therefore, we must not lose sight in driving productivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to ensure that there is continued investment in companies and workers so that our economy is vibrant and productive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Only when businesses do well, can our workers enjoy sustainable wage gains.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Training is essential to help our workers get those better jobs and better pay.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is tempting to reduce training costs during such times.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But these are longer-term investments in our workforce that will reap longer term benefits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We hope that the Government will continue to fund and maintain the SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We will also need businesses to rethink business models to capitalise on technology to increase productivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: NTUC has embarked on the proliferating the set-up of Company Training Committees (CTCs) to foster and engender transformation at the firm level.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: OTR can assist businesses to use innovation and technology move up the value chain.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Workers can be more productive as a result.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Particularly, I urge SMEs owners to consider participating in OTR Programmes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: SMEs hire the bulk of our workforce and are instrumental in helping a large proportion of our workers to get better wages.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Eligible SMEs may apply for grants extended by Enterprise Singapore to offset up to 80% of OTR costs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Government and the union stand ready to assist both workers and enterprises at every step of the way to boost productivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are not merely idle observers of rising costs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Raising productivity is key but we must also make sure that gains are shared fairly and equitably.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is an important tenet of our social compact.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are workers, especially lower-wage ones, in sectors where market forces work against them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: PWM has helped these workers to be paid better.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It also helps to keep wage disparity tighter.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We will expand into food services and waste management next year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We will need to study expanding into other areas more rapidly to help our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The support from the Government via the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme (PWCS) to help businesses cope with the increased cost of wages are vital in the interim.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Throughout the period of PWCS support, I hope businesses will use this period to devise new ways to attract local talent and increase productivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Businesses should tap on grants to increase productivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Examples of these grants – there are a lot of them – that seek to increase job productivity include the Productivity Solutions Grant which offers up to 80% support in the food services and retail sectors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is also the NTUC Company Training Committee Grant which provides funding support of up to 70% of qualifying costs for each project and aims to enhance business capabilities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I hope that the tripartite partners will persist in the implementation when the easier path might be to delay them in the face of rising costs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As for our vulnerable workers, such as mature workers, PWDs and ex-offenders, MOM will be extending Jobs Growth Incentive (JGI) to March 2023.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I hope that employers will continue to tap on the JGI to hire our vulnerable workers, who are very qualified as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Beyond 2023 March horizon, I also call on the Government to consider further extensions of the JGI if inflationary pressure has not eased by then.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Additional support for PWDs in the form of the Enabling Employment Credit, which offers employers wage offsets of up to 30% for eligible Singaporean PWDs should continue to ensure sufficient employment support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But we must at no point be under any delusion that Singapore is able to do all these without resources.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We could do all this because firstly, there are investments to create new and better jobs; two, we have the resources to invest in our workers and care for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This system has helped us grow our wages over the years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The economic and geopolitical imperatives to train and transform will be even greater as structural changes become deeper and more pervasive, economic conditions become more volatile, even more resources will be needed to help workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: So, we must keep faith in investing in our workers for the long run to protect them against inflation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Similarly, we must reject short-term solutions that harm longer-term viability.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Solutions such as consuming more of our NIRC now instead of investing them to meet future unpredictable challenges are very risky.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: More consumption today must also mean less to invest for future returns.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Sustainable wage growth is still the best protection against long-term inflation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: NTUC will do our part to help workers tide over challenging times.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The union has always stood ready to step up during times of need.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These are in addition to the support provided by the various unions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: NTUC and its social enterprises will continue to moderate the costs of living.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It was a mission that we took on since the formation of the cooperatives in 1970.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our social enterprises face the same cost pressures as any other businesses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
