text: We face the same cost increase in logistics, manpower and goods.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are in tradable sectors where there is the same competition for raw materials and manpower as other commercial entities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: NTUC FairPrice continues to benchmark prices and keeps food and daily essentials available and affordable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is constantly updating and enhancing its range of House Brands to offer better value and quality to meet the evolving needs of consumers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, late last year, NTUC FairPrice brought down the cost of Antigen Rapid Test (ART) kits by half to help relieve the financial burden on workers, including those rostered to go through routine rostered testing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is also the “Greater Value Everyday” campaign which consists of various discount and value schemes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, the Save Even More scheme sees groups such as the Pioneer and Merdeka Generations, our seniors, CHAS Blue card holders enjoying the same existing discount schemes from Monday to Friday.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Kopitiam and NTUC Foodfare launched a new initiative in May this year to help workers access cooked food and drinks at lower prices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: By the end of this year, 2.4 million NTUC members and NTUC Link members will be able to benefit from 10% savings when they pay use the NTUC FairPrice app for purchases at Kopitiam.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This initiative will apply across all FairPrice supermarkets, including FairPrice Online.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This basket of 500 key essential items is selected based on items that customers purchase frequently and serves the top-of-mind needs of customers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They comprise national brand, house brands, fresh fruits, vegetables and meat, staples, dairy, paper products and household cleaners – quite a lot.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The union will continue to actively monitor the impact of inflation and will work in tandem with the Government to enhance our efforts when required.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To combat the short-term impact of the GST increase, the Labour Movement is heartened that the Government has rolled out a comprehensive set of measures since the start of the year and will stand ready to help Singaporeans if things do not get better.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement will complement the Government’s effort to help Singaporeans cope.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: NTUC, along with its Social Enterprises, will continue to ensure that our workers and families have accessible, affordable and quality goods and services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We believe that a longer term and more sustainable approach for our workers and businesses to cope with the rising cost of living is through boosting skills and capabilities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We stand committed to work with the Government to help workers stay relevant with training and help businesses do even better.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.25 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.01 pm until 3.25 pm.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has basically put up two arguments against the Opposition.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, while the Government does not deny that it has ample revenue, it insists that much of the revenue is not to be used for this generation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, the GST is not regressive because the poor are compensated by GST vouchers, never mind the other Singaporeans, including the sandwich class, who have to pay more.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government, however, did not confirm or deny that figure.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do not want to raise the same questions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The time is better spent telling a story to illustrate what is happening and let Singaporeans decide.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many would remember the story about Ah Seng and his grandfather, Ah Gong, told by former Member of Parliament Lee Bee Wah.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, I will share one more episode with all of you.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   The Story of Ah Seng – Second Episode.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ah Seng’s parents died when he was very young and he was brought up by his grandfather.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ah Seng was not a prodigal son or a "see gui kia" who only knew how to get money from his grandfather.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ever since Ah Seng started working, he had always been giving his grandfather a large proportion of his salary.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After Ah Seng got married and had children, his expenses began to increase rapidly, but his grandfather continued to ask Ah Seng to increase his allowance.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Grandfather had his reasons, like he needed money to pay his wife's medical bills, or because he needed money to refurbish the ancestral homes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, all this while, Ah Seng carried a heavy financial burden and had limited cash savings.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the extended family was truly short of money, grandfather's requests would be reasonable.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But as Ah Seng grew older, he realised that the extended family, headed by his grandfather, was doing pretty well financially, as their ancestors had left behind many properties and assets.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the grandfather never revealed this to Ah Seng, and deliberately kept it as a secret.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All this while, Ah Seng, who had a strong notion of self-reliance, had not given much thought to the ancestral assets.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He did not complain even when he had to pay his grandfather the market price to purchase a house allocated to him out of the ancestral assets when he got married.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the time, the grandfather gave Ah Seng some money to help with the down payment, and Ah Seng borrowed money from banks to pay for the rest of the house.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After that, the grandfather continually invest the proceeds from the sale of the house that he received from Ah Seng.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As Ah Seng entered middle age, his career began to flounder and his income became unstable.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The cost of living also began to rise precipitously.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under such circumstances, when grandfather again asked Ah Seng to increase his allowance, Ah Seng felt aggrieved, and started to feel some discontent towards his grandfather.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, each time any family member questioned the grandfather about the ancestral assets, he would rage and call them spoilt children.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He would warn them not to spout nonsense.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Actually, Ah Seng agreed that they should leave behind more assets for the future generation, but not without addressing the urgent needs of the present generation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fellow Singaporeans, do you agree with the grandfather's behaviour?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If you are Ah Seng, would you agree to his grandfather's request for an increase in allowance?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Justice is in the hearts of the people.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: His story of Ah Gong and Ah Seng is very compelling.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: But it seems to only include two characters, which is Ah Gong and Ah Seng.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In this particular story, has he considered other characters, for example, other family members, friends, visitors who have come to the house to visit, from whom Ah Gong would have collected a fair share of collective to increase the fiscal capacity to further help Ah Seng.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Could he please clarify if he would consider including other characters in his particular story?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: As I have said in my speech at the beginning, there are other episodes to the story, so let me add in other episodes in other Sittings.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Personally, Mr Speaker, Sir, this debate is a difficult one and I am sure many of our colleagues here in the Chamber would agree.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: During my block visits and conversation with the residents of Pasir Ris-Punggol, cost of living, healthcare and taking care of our increasingly ageing population are issues that weigh heavily on their minds.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we can all try to understand what is going on in the world today and explain the confluence of reasons for the global inflation, or how the Singaporean dollar has strengthened to reduce the net impact of inflation, all these explanations fade away when at the end of the day the price of our grocery bill is more expensive than what it was previously.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Prospects in 2023 do not look too rosy either.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Economists expect inflation rates to ease but will remain high at 3.5%.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This comes with a forecasted slowdown in GDP growth.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This was in tandem with a worsening outlook for the global economy and stubbornly high inflation globally.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In my conversations with Pasir Ris residents, across the board, high inflation rates, cost of living and healthcare were top on everyone's worry.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In a Public Policy Forum with youths at Pasir Ris East, our youths were concerned about the cost of living, affordability of healthcare for our seniors and the load of supporting our rapidly ageing population across a smaller base.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One of them, Mr Charles Chow, a young working professional, is concerned for the fact that four working adults are supporting one senior now; but by 2030, only two working adults will support one senior.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What are the future financial challenges for working adults if this trend continues?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He wonders how we can distribute the costs of providing affordable healthcare among a larger group of taxpayers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Last week, in a dialogue session with more than 70 members in the Malay/Muslim community through M3 Pasir Ris-Punggol, the top three concerns they had for the community were: rising cost, including assistance for low-income families; healthcare cost for our ageing population; and education for students from lower-income families.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of the residents in my ward are between the ages of 55 and 65.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Their children have only recently begun working, their homes will be paid for in the next few years, they have extensive work experience and they plan to retire soon.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, present inflation rates and rising costs of healthcare raise a real concern that their retirement account would prove insufficient.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They worry that they would be a burden to their own children after retirement.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They are in their mid-30s or 40s with school-going kids and have relocated from their BTOs in Punggol or Sengkang to Pasir Ris to be closer to their parents who will retire soon.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They are concerned about the rising cost of living for their family and the assistance available to care for their elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They feel sandwiched between their family and responsibility for their parents.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we fund this increasing healthcare cost?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Do we lessen spending on social development, security and external relations or economic development or do we need to increase our revenue sources and redistribute resources more fairly to create a more inclusive society?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We all agree that more must be done to keep healthcare affordable and provide greater assistance to lower-income families.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We want more to be done without overburdening the lower- and middle-income.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We believe that those who have been blessed with more should give back more to society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, what are our options to provide the necessary healthcare support for our rapidly ageing population while minimising the impact on the majority of Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In MOF's analysis of revenue and expenditure based on FY2021, about 70% of Singapore's revenue comes from NIRC, corporate tax, income tax and Goods and Services Tax.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In his Budget speech, Deputy Prime Minister Wong mentioned the consideration of all the other types of taxes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, I will not touch on them here.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I would like to provide a perspective from the industry on corporate tax and, in particular, the impact of Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS 2.0) and if this can be a dependable alternative to raise the additional income we require to finance the increasing healthcare cost.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I lead strategy and programme execution, including where to invest, for a company that has a 30% global market share for the maintenance repair and overhaul of aerospace jet engines.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In my previous role, I was also involved in making decisions of expansion plans for a global multinational company (MNC).

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: My portfolio included setting up new manufacturing facilities and retrofitting factories that build advanced jet engines in UK, Germany, Canada and Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Under Pillar One, 25% of the residual profits – defined as profit in excess of 10% of revenue – will be allocated away from where the economic activities are conducted to where the markets are.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given Singapore's small domestic market in comparison to those around us as well as our role as a regional hub for MNCs to do business from, there is an expected net outflow of tax revenue as tax is allocated away to the markets where the MNCs are serving.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In his earlier speeches, Deputy Prime Minister Wong mentioned the magnitude of fiscal impact would only be clear after international negotiations have been concluded and it has not.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: By increasing the minimum effective tax rate, we may collect more corporate tax and hence, may just possibly increase tax revenue.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, this truly depends on how other governments and companies react.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Though collectively planned for in 2023, implementing BEPS 2.0 across 135 OECD countries will be difficult and uncertain.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There is no clear timeline for implementation or how governments will react to it.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Should we be the first to implement BEPS 2.0 by hiking corporate taxes willingly ahead of others and foregoing this competitive lever of our economy, especially at a time where other countries are aggressively courting more business investments to aid in their economic recovery?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How will this impact our ability to attract investments?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Should we put our country's competitiveness at risk since we do not know when and how other countries will implement the changes?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If we raise corporate taxes to the same level as other countries or worse, ahead of other countries who are competing for the same investment, we would lose this competitive lever for attracting foreign investments.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is of no doubt that with all the headwinds I have mentioned, we will have to do something and spend on non-tax incentives to restore and enhance our business competitiveness to continue to attract foreign investments when we lose preferential tax rates as one of our competitive levers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We will also need to spend more on programmes, such as the Productivity Solutions Grant, Enterprise Development Grant, CTO-as-a-Service and many more grants, to help our SMEs grow and develop capabilities that would instill investor confidence that this tiny dot of ours, our Singapore, has the ecosystem that will enable their investments to grow and flourish and, most importantly, provide good jobs to our people despite not having preferential tax rates.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There is also the uncertainty of how businesses and governments will react when they lose this competitive lever, too.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The business world is neither simple nor static.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Businesses and governments will react to this tax equalisation through the provision of grants or corporate schemes to continue to attract investments whenever they lose preferential tax as a lever to attract investments.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Businesses have a choice to make and these are not binary choices of to invest or not to invest.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Businesses can choose to slow down their growth, especially slow down their growth in Singapore, choose to not grow their operations in Singapore, diversify elsewhere or, worse, exit Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Any of these decisions will hurt our workers and our economy and that has a secondary effect of lowering our tax collection further.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, taking into consideration the uncertainties – the uncertainty of when it is to be implemented across all the OECD member states, uncertainty of the net income we can receive from it, uncertainty of how businesses and governments will react – how can we have the confidence to rely on this uncertain revenue source to finance something as certain and as critical as the healthcare needs of our ageing population?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The real question is, Mr Speaker, Sir, will there be a net increase in income from corporate tax such that gains in BEPS 2.0 alone can be sufficient to make up the “hole left behind by not raising GST”?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Is the implementation of BEPS 2.0 a viable and sustainable alternative to GST in paying for our increasing healthcare costs?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: My worry, Mr Speaker, Sir: one in four Singaporeans will be above the age of 65 in 2030 is a certainty; 200,000 Singaporeans will be above the age of 80 by 2030 is a certainty; our increasing healthcare cost is a certainty.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we risk the expenditure of something so certain with an uncertain income source?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Do we want to take the risk and jeopardise with the healthcare of our population?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If corporate tax is not a suitable alternative at present, then how about GST?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When a tourist is having a meal at our restaurants or booked for himself a 5-star hotel, if he spends $1,000 for a three-day stay in one of our hotels, that additional tax income contributes to paying for our healthcare cost.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As fellow Parliamentary colleague, Mr Saktiandi Supaat, mentioned earlier, which other taxation tool allows us to tax a non-residential population so effectively?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Though they can claim tax refunds for goods that they purchased, the additional tax that they pay for services contribute to our tax income directly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Nevertheless, as much as GST allows us to earn more from visitors, we must do as much as we can to assist the middle and lower income, such as through the Assurance Package, the cost of living and GST packages.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The enhanced GST cash vouchers, GST U-Save rebates to offset utilities, S&CC rebates, MediSave top-ups for seniors and GST Seniors' Bonus means that many Singaporeans pay GST below the headline rate.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   Inflation is at an all-time high in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In my conversations with Pasir Ris residents, including those from the Malay/Muslim community, many said that they are worried about the high inflation rates, cost of living and healthcare.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: During a dialogue session with more than 70 members of the community through M3@Pasir Ris-Punggol network, the top three concerns that they faced were the need to take care of the elderly, assistance for low-income families who are facing increasingly rising costs, and education for students from low-income families.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I understand and note that the issue of GST hike is complicated, especially with the increase in the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, the fact is, this GST increase will be channelled to take better care of our seniors whose number is increasing; besides meeting the rising healthcare expenses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Almost one in five Singaporeans are aged 65 and above, and this figure will increase to about one in four by 2030.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is a threefold increase in 10 years.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That is almost 10 times increase compared to the cost in 2012.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, we need to prepare a revenue stream right now to ensure that we will have sufficient resources.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: First, the Government will fully absorb the GST on education and healthcare, which will receive public subsidy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The GST Voucher Scheme, which has three components - cash payment, Medisave top-ups and U-Save rebates - will be enhanced when the GST is raised.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will fully offset the GST for retiree households living in 1-room to 3-room HDB flats, significantly offset the GST for retiree households living in 4-room to 5-room HDB flats and offset about half of the GST for low-income households without seniors.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, the high level of inflation, coupled with the needs of our ageing population, is top of everyone’s worry.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is of no doubt that, as our population ages, our healthcare cost will increase and we must be prepared for it.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We all believe in a fair and inclusive society where the lower income families should receive more assistance.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong has shared many alternative taxation tools considered in previous debates.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With regard to corporate tax and the impact of BEPS 2.0, from an industry perspective, when Singapore loses the competitive lever of preferential tax rates, we will definitely have to do something and spend more on non-tax incentives to restore and enhance our business competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With all the uncertainties in implementing BEPS 2.0, the only thing certain is that even if there is an increase in revenue from corporate taxes, there will not be a direct flowthrough of revenue to income.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we then depend on something so uncertain to fund our increasing healthcare cost?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the right rebates, like the enhanced GST Voucher, U-Save rebates, S&CC rebates, Seniors' Bonus, CDC vouchers, just to name a few, we can delay the impact of the GST increase to many of our residents.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In fact, the lower 10% of the population does not pay GST at all.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: GST, being a consumption tax, is one of the ways to obtain revenue.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: More GST is being borne by the higher income group.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr H, aged 68, stays with his wife, Mdm L, aged 63, in a 3-room HDB flat.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr H left his job as a taxi driver in 2020 when his wife was diagnosed with kidney failure and needed to start dialysis.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, he takes care of their eight-year-old granddaughter.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They were very worried about financial challenges if Mdm L was not able to continue working.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Other costs include half-yearly treatment costs and medicines amounting to about $600.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With various Government subsidies and assistance schemes, they can cope with the dialysis costs and daily expenses.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Their granddaughter is also receiving financial assistance from MOE.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But Mr H shares with me that he is very concerned about the depletion of his and his wife's MediSave accounts.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Currently, they are depending on their MediSave to pay for their medical bills.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As they get older and may not be able to continue working, the contributions to MediSave may stop.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: By then, it will be very tough for them to cope with their medical bills.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr H hopes that the Government would consider topping up higher amounts for the MediSave accounts of the vulnerable elderly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that there can be more support and subsidies for outpatient treatments of chronic illnesses through the existing CHAS scheme for our Pioneer Generation and Merdeka Generation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   In view of rising medical costs, and that one of the key reasons why we have to increase GST is that our ageing population requires more support, I would also like to ask for higher withdrawal limits for Medisave.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I also hope that the Government can provide more support and subsidies for outpatient treatments of chronic illnesses through the existing CHAS scheme, for our Pioneer Generation and Merdeka Generation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): Other than the elderly, I can understand the burden of the sandwich class as I speak to many of them during my walkabouts.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They feel very stretched by the increasing costs of living.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Inflation is affecting their incomes which may not have kept pace with the increase in costs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Separately, I would like to suggest that the Government send each Singaporean an annual consolidated statement of the various subsidies, top-ups and cash payouts he or she receives in the mail.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This statement totaling all the benefits should also be available in the Singpass app such that our citizens will know how much assistance or support they have received.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is important that our people obtain the correct perspective on how revenue collected and redistributed helps to assist the less privileged in our community so that no one gets left behind.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our nation is built upon a mutually supportive and enabling ecosystem, of which a cohesive and united people are the foundation.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong had earlier this year, in his Budget round-up speech, explained why this cannot replace the GST increase.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: For today, I wish to comment on their NIRC proposal.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But Sir, before I do so, I think it is even more important to re-examine why we are having a GST hike.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Of course, we all know a GST hike is never politically popular at any point in time anywhere.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But in Singapore, the PAP has always done what we think is in the best interest of Singapore now and for successive generations; sometimes, regardless of the political cost.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: That is why we are where we are today.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: That should not be an inter-generation transfer of liabilities such that one generation pays for the services consumed by another generation.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is surely not a "pay as you go" arrangement that we see in other countries.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is the slippery slope that we must not go down and there are many examples of this elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Eventually, it pits one generation against another and leads to society fissuring and even fracturing along generation lines.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If we drop to 40% to reserves, what is there to say we cannot drop to 30% or even 20%?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I must say 50-50 is not rocket science, and I am the first to admit empirically, it feels like the right thing to do.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We are an Asian society and generally speaking, our forebears have tried very hard to give us a better life than what they went through.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is possible only because they consumed less than what they produced and left us with the rest.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We should continue this good practice of leaving something for our descendants.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: So, at this juncture, I would like to take a pause and comment on some of the speeches that were made earlier.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The hon Member Mr Louis Chua likened a GST increase to scoring an own goal when you are 5-0 down in football.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: When he said that, I am reminded of the Suzuki Cup semi-finals last year, on Christmas Day, where I was there with Minister Edwin Tong and which Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong also mentioned during his Budget speech.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In that game on Christmas Day last year, our Lions lost 4-2 against Indonesia.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We had one man sent off, two men sent off, three men sent off.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But the Young Lions battled, they were clearing shots off the line, they defended stoutly and they were throwing bodies all around.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Not the way that Mr Chua has spoken about – conceding an own goal or scoring an own goal when you are 5-0 down.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim also made mention of over-saving for our reserves.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We are not just saving, we are re-investing.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We are then flowing it back to the NIRC of future generations.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Just a short while ago, I see a group of students in our audience; they just left.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But why do you think even in such turbulent times, we are able to invest in education, to invest for the future?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is precisely because of the reserves that our forefathers had given us.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There is no such thing as under-saving or over-saving for a small country like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We have to save as much as we can, and I dare say, for a small country like ours, do what you can and do not ever use that word "over-saving", please.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I will go back to my speech now.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If I have time, I would like to say something on Mr Leong Mun Wai's speech but let us see.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I am sure the Government knows that both in their hearts and their minds.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Here I am reminded of what a doctor friend told me.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The difference between analgesia – I hope I pronounced it correctly – analgesia and pain relief.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: For example, an anesthetist is trained to achieve analgesia in a patient undergoing surgery.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But when a patient is in this state, he needs constant monitoring and this consumes a lot of resources.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is not possible to have a long period of time whereby a patient feels no pain.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is because pain is a sensation and not to have any sensation is dangerous.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: While we do not like pain at all, a little pain is necessary because it is what makes us alert, it is what keeps us alive.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: To have no sensation of pain, unless induced by a doctor through anesthetic intervention for a short while, is not good at all.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: A good example is a person with badly controlled diabetes.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Often, he has no sensation in his lower extremities because his nerves have died due to the scourge of diabetes.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Not just pain, he actually also feels nothing at all in the area where the nerves have died.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As a result, he may not know he has developed bad diabetic ulcers, which can sadly end up with an amputation of a part of the leg.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: He may even die from these painless diabetic ulcers.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: So, in summary, only the deceased feel nothing for a long period of time.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is therefore neither possible nor advisable that the Government shield Singaporeans from difficult economic conditions worldwide, so that they feel no pain at all.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is also not responsible for the Government of this generation to spend more than its fair share so that this generation of Singaporeans feel no pain.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The can is kicked down the road and subsequent generations have to feel additional pain because of the profligacy that takes place now.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I know this sounds somewhat harsh, but reality is like that.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We must be prudent so that we are always resilient, no matter what or how the global climate is.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Only then can we bounce back from difficult challenges and grow even stronger in the future.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But it is also vital that the Government also feels for and understands the pain of Singaporeans during such challenging times.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: What the PAP aims to do is to reduce the pain, as in providing effective and substantial pain relief.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But we cannot provide analgesia so that we do not feel, at all, the adverse conditions around us.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: That would obtund us to the point that we may have a festering wound threatening our lives in the long term and yet we are not aware of it.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We may then die from it eventually, or at the very least, we may need drastic intervention not unlike chopping off a part of our limbs.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: That would be a disastrous outcome that we need to prevent.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Yet, we do so in a way such that Singaporeans remain alert, sensitive and even quickened to the challenges and threats around us.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But I must say, this does not stop the Government from intervening decisively to help families and individuals to lessen the pain in these trying times.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And I think that the Government has shown, through the years, that no matter how challenging the internal or external environment is, we will continue to support Singapore and Singaporeans on the cost of living here.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The question is whether we, as a country, are better off and more resilient if we take this approach?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Or are we better off if we take the PAP’s approach, which is to keep the country alert to dangers and challenges, while we give relief to those who are suffering more, as we forge ahead through these difficult waters?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: (In Mandarin):   Earlier, Mr Leong Mun Wai shared a story about Ah Gong and Ah Seng.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Of course, he is the author of the story, and we cannot stop him from writing the story as he pleases.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: So basically, Mr Leong is saying that this Ah Gong comes from a very rich family and he keeps taking money from Ah Seng until Ah Seng is out of breath.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But I want to share with him this saying, I do not know if he has heard of it before - "you can raise a child for 100 years and you will worry about his welfare for 99 years." We are an Asian society.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We take care of our children and grandchildren for 100 years and for 99 years we keep worrying about him.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In an Asian society like Singapore, are there stories as he has mentioned?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Of course, there are, but they are rare.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: He keeps talking about how Ah Gong tries to collect money from Ah Seng until Ah Seng is out of breath.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I think that this is very rare in our society.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I do not know whether he has heard of another phrase – "A thousand gold can’t buy being poor at a young age", which means that if you are not rich when you are young, when you grow up, you will appreciate what you have and treasure the people around you more.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Hence, I found it very hard to believe his story.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Perhaps Ah Gong is trying to teach the grandson, or to save for his grandson to prepare for his education in the future and so on.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: So, I think the story Mr Leong told is very extreme.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I believe my colleague, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, has a clarification as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I just want to ask the hon Member Mr Sitoh Yih Pin, he said that some of our proposals are analgesic and anesthetic and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If that is the case, would the hon Member agree that the Support Package is also an anesthetic and it is better to have pain – no pain, no gain?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I do not see how the Support Packages can be "no pain".

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: The support packages are meant to help our fellow citizens to get over this period.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I noticed the Workers' Party kept saying "You are trying to fan the inflation".

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Yes, I think the Government implementing the GST in this difficult inflationary time.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: But please bear in mind that GST is also a consumption tax, in the sense that it is charged from the spend.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: So, I think the Assurance Package, GST Voucher is meant to help Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I do not see his point that it is meant to be "no pain" at all.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I am sorry, I missed the Member's point.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My point is that if I understood his speech correctly, he is saying that measures to ameliorate the negative impact of GST on the population are, in a way, kicking the can down the road or somehow dishonest because actually the population should feel the pain.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And we should not try to take measures that are alternatives to that – even though there are viable alternatives that we believe, which we have put forward as proposals, relating to NIR, relating to land sales, for example – we should not take that route.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Rather, we should allow the population to experience more pain.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: That is what I understood what the Member was saying.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, in that light, I would like to ask him whether some of the ameliorating measures that the Government has proposed will also fall into the same category.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: What I am saying is that we are all going through difficult times.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I did not say the assistance packages are not helpful.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: In fact, I think they are very helpful and the Government is targeting it at the people who need it most.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I did not say we deserve to go through this pain.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: What I am saying is that in these turbulent times of calamity, we have to bond together as a nation and we have to go through this together – 同甘共苦的精神, the spirit of sharing weal and woe – if the Member knows what I mean.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I always thought that academics were the only ones to conceive of unrealistic scenarios, but I was somehow shocked to hear Member Sitoh Yih Pin say that there is no such thing as over-saving.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If we take this argument to his own logical extreme, why do we not simply just lower our NIRC ceiling to 0% and not tap on NIRC at all?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If we think there is no such thing as over-saving, is he saying that the Government of 2008, having tapped on a lower percentage, actually under-saved?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If so, then, in his own words, can he provide the empirically verifiable evidence that they, in fact, did so?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I think if you were to play the tape, I said for a small country like Singapore, do not talk about over-saving.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I said for a small country like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I am reminded of 1997, during the Asian Financial Crisis.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: The countries around us – their currencies all collapsed.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: In the summer of 1998, the SAR Hong Kong government, with the backing of Beijing, had to come in to defend the Hong Kong dollar and to defend the Hang Seng Index.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: So, for a small country like Singapore, saving is a virtue and we should continue to save.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: As far as I checked, in 2008, it was the same country of Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In 2008, as far as I believe, the Government altered its NIRC contribution percentage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We do not have, at least on the record, the specific shares.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, I am not talking about China here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This PAP Government, which was in power in Singapore at the time, in 2008, altered the NIRC share.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I completely agree that the NIRC system is a good system.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Mr Leon Perera asked a question earlier after Mr Liang Eng Hwa's speech.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I think he asked about what if 50-50 is not enough.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think the question was really, if we heard the hon Member correctly in his speech, the hon Member said that there can be no such thing, in theory, by definition, as over-saving for a small country like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Is that the Member's position or is that not the Member's position?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: For a small country like Singapore, with a limited population, with no natural resources, saving is a virtue.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I do not think we should grouse about over-saving.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think the question has not been answered.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My question to the hon Member Sitoh Yih Pin is – do you or do you not believe that there can be such a thing as over-saving, in theory, for a small country like Singapore?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I said for a small country like Singapore, saving must be a virtue and as far as we can, we can continue to save, not just for future generations but for a rainy day.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Does he not think that savings should be a virtue or does he think that we should saving now?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I think, Mr Sitoh, I would like to save some time and move on to Ms Jessica Tan.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With inflation and households facing rising prices in many areas, such as energy and food, many of our residents continue to express concerns with the higher cost of living.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think many Members have expressed that as well.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Although Singapore's GST rate, even at 9%, is amongst the lowest in the world, an increase in GST will still impact all Singaporeans and all Singaporean households, regardless of income levels.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Hence, this is adding to the anxiety of many of our residents over the cost of living.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, if the situation arises, with the sustained trend of rising prices and inflation, I do hope that there will be timely reviews and adjustments to rising cost of living with the Assurance Package as it is dispersed over five years.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is to ensure that the support given does, indeed, provide the extent of the support, as it is intended to offset the increase in the additional GST.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In my Budget debate speech earlier this year, I had highlighted the point about the eligibility criteria for the support, which I wish to reiterate.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The annual value (AV) of residence or your home address is used as the main criterion for means testing and eligibility for many of our support schemes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I agree that we need to do means testing and that those who are less well-off and vulnerable must get more support.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In the cash payout component of the Assurance Package, there is a change in the eligibility criteria where eligibility and the amount of the cash payout component of the Assurance Package are based on annual income and property ownership, instead of the annual value of residence.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This means that retirees who do not have an income and those who are not well-off and live with well-meaning relatives or friends in private condominiums or houses, who usually would not be eligible for such payouts, will now be getting the cash payouts to offset the additional GST increase.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I was looking at the $700 – the lowest of the categories in these payouts – just to get a sense of what that means for the individual.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It may not cover everything, but it is not insignificant.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And it is also just one of the components.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While I do not disagree that the value of the property reflects one's means, I have seen the need for support amongst some of our residents who live in properties that are above the annual value threshold criterion.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A point that I have raised several times in this House is the application of the annual value criterion for those who live with their extended families in properties with annual values above the eligibility criterion of $21,000.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These persons could be elderly parents or siblings who live with relatives as they need care or cannot afford housing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In several of these cases, they do not have means.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But because of their residential address, they do not qualify for the various support schemes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the trend of smaller families as well, people marrying later, there are also many more couples who have to provide for both their young children and senior parents and relatives.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do have such families in my constituency who live in private properties with an annual value of between $21,000 and $30,000.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For example, take the GST Voucher – Cash (Seniors' Bonus) in the Assurance Package.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Seniors or retirees living in properties of annual values above $21,000 will not be eligible.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am not asking that means testing or the annual value be removed.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What I am asking is whether it can be calibrated to allow eligibility for those living with extended family members but do not own the property or can there be a higher AV threshold with a lower cash bonus for retirees that own the property but require support.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For the sandwich generation, can there also be calibration to allow for higher AV thresholds to allow eligibility for the support schemes if they do meet the annual income criterion?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For the sandwich generation who live in private properties, if the seniors who live with them or who they support are eligible for support schemes, this will help cushion some of the rising cost of care and the rising cost of living that many have expressed today.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Although not directly related to the GST increase, ECDA's recent announcement of the lower fee caps for preschool from January next year at anchor operators and partner operators is, indeed, welcomed as it will help parents in the sandwich group manage cost.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Together with the other tax measures in Budget 2022, it will give the revenue required to fund rising expenditures needed for social spending.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Government's approach ensures that we start building the funding required today, now, while delaying the impact of the GST for most Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I have heard quite a bit of the speeches and there were quite a lot of asks to delay the GST increase.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, let us not miss the bigger picture.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The bigger picture is we need that funding.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We can say, delay the impact, but what about the funding?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If we delay the GST, we delay the building up of the funding.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, what do we do when we need it?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Scramble and figure out something at that point in time?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In my speech, I have given focus to the "sandwiched generation", as they have to care for both their young children and aged parents and relatives and will bear greater financial strain with rising cost.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While many do live in HDB flats and qualify for most of the components of the Assurance Package, there are those that live in private property that are above the Annual Value (AV) threshold for eligibility.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I have also highlighted seniors living with relatives in private property, but do not own these properties.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These seniors are not eligible for the GST Voucher (Senior Bonus) but may be less well-off than a senior living in an HDB flat that they own but eligible for the GST Cash Voucher (Senior Bonus).

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This, together with the right support for those who are disadvantaged, will ensure good opportunities for all to do well.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And I think that is what we are all debating today; not just the GST increase.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is especially so, given the heightened inflation and concerns around cost of living.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: My residents are feeling the pinch, and the bad news is that inflation is expected to be prolonged this time.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The GST hike was first announced in 2018 and five years in the making.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We have had many debates in Parliament, including today.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: And speaking on behalf of my residents, I have made repeated appeals asking the Government to consider alternative revenue sources, delay the increase and provide support to Singaporeans to cope with the impact.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This year alone, I raised such questions on five separate occasions.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There are many meritorious commitments made by the Government, including support for parents dealing with childcare and education.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We just heard about HDB subsidies for young couples in the form of housing subsidies – the big deficit that HDB is recording.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For our workers in the form of higher wages we have all been championing, for all the upskilling initiatives and for the significant investments in the Singapore Green Plan.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: And we all in this House, have said yes to all of these.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Since I became a Member of Parliament in 2011, I have witnessed first-hand, the positive impact on our seniors and their families, of successive healthcare support schemes such as MediShield Life, CHAS and the enhanced CHAS, Pioneer Generation Package and the Merdeka Generation Package.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Furthermore, the pandemic experience reminds us how crucial it is to continue to invest in our healthcare system in order to be able to respond effectively to future pandemics and emergencies.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The hard truth is that all these need to be paid for.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Government has singled out increasing healthcare costs as a primary driver for the need to increase GST.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We have had many debates in this House, like I have said, on how we should pay for these higher expenditures.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Members of the Opposition have repeated called for more of our reserves to be used to meet our rising expenditure.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It would be unfair to future generations if we were to raid our reserves and leave them with less.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Indeed, since 2016, I have observed that our reserves had already become the single largest contributor to the Budget.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The fiscal strength of Singapore is built upon a diversity of revenue streams.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Increasing our dependency on the reserves to fund expenditures will further tilt the balance towards unhealthy concentration risk.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It would be wrong for us to contemplate taking more and leaving less for the next generation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is particularly at a time when the world is getting more divided and more dangerous, because of contentious geopolitics, disrupted supply chains and existential climate change challenges.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Those coming after us would need more, not less, of a buffer of financial resources, to secure their future.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The choices, unfortunately, that he laid out point to the inevitable increase, however reluctant we may be to support it.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But the Government has committed to cushion the impact of GST increase with the Assurance Package, covering at least five years of additional GST expenses for majority of Singaporeans households and about 10 years for lower-income households.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We have also seen there are also enhancements to the Permanent GST Voucher scheme, to provide continuing offsets for GST expenses of lower- to middle-income households and most retiree households, therefore providing beyond the transitional period covered by the Assurance Package.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Such actions by the Government go some way to assure fellow Singaporeans that our Government has our back.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I note that these support measures are funded from better-than-expected fiscal outcomes in the first half of FY2022, with no draw on Past Reserves.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Over 60% of net GST is paid by the top 20% of Singaporean households, foreigners living in Singapore and tourists-net of refunds.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Then the next question usually comes, "Is Singapore getting too expensive and therefore less competitive?" After all, the wealthy are globally mobile – and with so many schemes from around the world wooing them, will they still choose Singapore in which to invest, build their business and bring good jobs?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Keep in mind that GST is not the only tax they face – for example, the foreigners are subjected to 30% additional buyers stamp duty to purchase property, over five times more for hospital ward and up to 70 times more to attend Singapore Secondary school.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I have spoken on numerous occasions in the past about the premium that Singapore commands in a volatile and uncertain world, because we enjoy the rule of law, stability, safety and international connectivity.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This has not been lost on investors and wealthy families who choose to base themselves out of Singapore and they will continue to do their calculations.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We must therefore continue to ensure that Singapore remains their destination of choice, even if we cannot be the most price-competitive location.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I often hear middle-income residents share the challenge they face to sustain their financial commitments and the frustrations of not being able to maintain their way of life.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They worry about the adequacy of their safety nets, should they lose their jobs or suffer a life-changing event.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We must do more to support this group and give them greater assurance.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For those who have seen the award-winning film, Parasite, we would be familiar with the basement apartments in South Korea.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When the floodwaters rush in, people living in these humble dwellings get their homes destroyed and, worse, lose their lives.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thankfully, the South Korean government has recently vowed to move people out of these homes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What rising floodwaters are to subterranean South Korean homes, the rising costs of living are to Singaporeans at the bottom of the socioeconomic ladder.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When it hits, the lives and livelihoods of those at the bottom are the first to be put to the sword – all the way up to the middle of the ladder, we have Singaporeans up to their necks with surging prices on living necessities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Of course, I could have spared the analogy, for this is basic economic theory.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Yes, basic, but, for many of us, it merely remains in theory.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For lower- to middle-income working Singaporeans, rising GST rates will be felt in the flesh.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These measures will tide Singaporeans over fiscal challenges as they navigate the rising cost of living in the near-term, and the Union brothers and sisters I have spoken with are grateful for this support on behalf of our Singaporean workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, while such assistance provides relief, we must continue to look to policies that imbue resilience.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Rising costs are, undoubtedly, a perennial issue – every generation reminisces about the prices of their kopi, a bowl of noodles back in their day.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: PWCS served to encourage salary increments for lower-wage workers despite the poor macroeconomic climate, incentivising, therefore, lower-wage workers’ investment in the development of their craft.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As the cost of living rises, we are confident that Singaporeans will be well-resourced to match its demands for greater productivity in a sustainable gain-sharing ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, the Labour Movement will continue to play its part to help seniors and other Singaporeans to "stretch their dollar" through its social enterprises.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This includes special discounts on basic necessities, such as groceries at our Fairprice outlets, tailored insurance policies with NTUC Income, and meals at Kopitiam.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I note that there are now $3 options nestled in most Kopitiam stalls in my Division, and there are many popular food items enjoyed by many, such as cai png, carrot cake, fishball noodles, mee goreng and chicken macaroni soup.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Aside from these wage workers, there is also a slice of business owners and the self-employed who may be adversely impacted by the rising rates of GST.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While established corporations have elaborate pricing models to capture profits amidst the volatile economic climate, small business owners in Singapore feel a special affinity for their customer base and have an often overlooked obligation to their regulars to keep prices down.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is not uncommon to hear residents name their favourite food after their associated prices.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Think the “$2.50 chicken rice” or the “$1 banana leaf nasi lemak”.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Those dishes just have a special ring to it.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In our communities, small business owners who have fought to keep their prices down to keep serving their loyal customers are celebrated as community stalwarts, and treasure this trust more than just gouging profits.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As their suppliers pass the increasing costs of goods down to these small business owners in light of the rising GST rates, small business owners can, at best, apologetically raise their prices, or, at worst, absorb these costs out of their pockets to their own personal detriment.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This dilemma is one unique to small business owners in Singapore and need not be the one that we put them through if we pull the right policy levers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the same vein, our self-employed persons in Singapore, including taxi drivers, private hire drivers, who are generally unable to set their own prices, are also not GST-registered.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our drivers from the National Taxi Association and the National Private Hire Vehicles Association have told me that they are worried about the impending GST increments and thus affecting their daily takings and livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The costs of doing business would go up, from larger dollar items, such as fuel, car rentals, insurance, to the smallest of purchases essential to their businesses, such as masks and even sanitation wipes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This discernment in the application of GST will go a long way to supporting our SMEs and the self-employed who might feel cornered by the GST increase.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Mandarin):   I believe that many members of the public can feel the impact of the recent price adjustments.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the gradual increase in the cost of living, every household will face different pressures, with low-income households facing a more severe impact.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Similarly, SMEs will find it more difficult to balance their revenue and expenditure than large enterprises.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Of course, the biggest challenge is probably faced by self-employed workers such as our taxi and private hire car uncles and aunties.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These elderly and frail drivers are hardworking, but do not have the protection of a GST registration, but they have to bear the pressure of inflation on their own, just like big companies.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With rising prices, I believe we have seen a reduction in the number of times we take a cab and in our financial capability.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This may bring us some inconvenience, but to taxi drivers, what is affected is their ability to afford food, medical fees and rent.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Businesses that are unable to raise prices will have to use their own money to absorb these costs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is a reality that every elderly taxi driver must face.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Are we not raising taxes for the common prosperity of all?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Then protecting the rice bowls of the self-employed and the SMEs should be our duty.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Labour Movement continues to be committed to working with the Government to ensure that making this investment into our common Singaporean future does not disproportionately aggrieve overlooked slices of Singaporeans as I have outlined.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is without a doubt that Singaporeans will have greater social spending needs in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we also have to ensure this tax hike does not lead to fraud and profiteering.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The first set of clarifications has to do with missing trader fraud.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The person does not need to know of the specified arrangement or any details of the plan.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In other words, this offence seems to require knowledge of a fraudulent purpose only in the abstract.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister explain how knowledge of fraudulent purpose should be established if it cannot be shown that the individual knew of the specified arrangement or any details of the plan at all?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The culpability for this strict-liability offence is lower and this offence attracts lower penalties than the one for participation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Arguably, the actions of a sole proprietor, partner or director in allowing their entity to be used for missing trader fraud may amount to assisting or receiving instructions to carry out the fraud.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will IRAS publish guidelines, similar to the UK tax agency’s document on “How to spot missing trader VAT fraud”?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will IRAS offer rewards upon request for those reporting missing trader fraud as part of its existing whistleblower programme?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These guidelines and assurances will make it easier for businesses to comply in good faith and for whistleblowers to do the right thing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second set of clarifications relates to the Committee Against Profiteering (CAP).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many residents are concerned that businesses will use the GST hike as an excuse to raise prices further and result in an even higher increase in the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: CAP investigates complaints about businesses that use the GST hike as an excuse to raise prices of essential products and services.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It has said that it may “make public” businesses that profiteer by using the GST hike as a pretext.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister explain whether CAP has the power to publicly name businesses that were found to have profiteered?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, when describing the cases of profiteering, when should CAP name the businesses involved and when should it not?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Profiteers should face the strong deterrent of public scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Naming these businesses also gives the public the confidence that profiteers will face consequences and encourages good-faith reports, which strengthens CAP’s goal of increasing transparency.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will we consider making it a default practice to publicly name businesses that are found to have profiteered?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This should cover not only reports that CAP has already received but also those it will receive in the coming months, as the GST hike takes effect.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This has enabled us to overcome challenges and pursue opportunities with confidence.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In both situations, Singapore was able to land safely due to our Government’s fiscal prudence and decisive actions.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While we have emerged from COVID-19 better than many countries, many challenges lie ahead.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Our nation’s expenditures are projected to grow to meet rising needs.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: These must be financed by tax receipts which are impacted by an increasingly gloomy economic outlook.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC) framework is being debated in this House.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I want to add my piece to say that I caution against the seemingly attractive suggestion to spend more from our investment returns and save less.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This easy way out is not a solution to this GST Bill proposed.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Investment experts have highlighted the declining trade liberalisation, increasing geopolitical uncertainties, along with the unwinding of a decade-long quantitative easing.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The era of cheap money for borrowing is over.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: If one borrows to invest, one also needs to price in the higher risks.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In other words, businesses and investors are faced potentially with lower returns, on average, on a risk-adjusted basis.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The world has changed dramatically in the recent past.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As such, we need to take heed that “past returns are not a guarantee of future performance”.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This context is relevant when we apply our minds and talk about the NIRC framework.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As this framework allows the Government to spend up to half of the long-term expected real returns on invested net assets, can the Deputy Prime Minister clarify if MOF has factored the known macroeconomic headwinds into the long-run expected returns and, if so, does MOF expect lower funding available for our upcoming Budget?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Also, given the challenging investment environment, what are the plans to steadily grow our reserves, to increase the dollar returns available for higher expenditures in the longer term?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The backdrop of the current investment climate calls for the need to uphold prudence and discipline in NIRC, so that the returns from our reserves can continue to be a key source of funding proportionate to the higher expected expenditures that are to come.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While I am convinced that the GST increase is required to support higher expenditure, I am also concerned about its impact on my residents and fellow Singaporeans, given inflationary pressures which are driving up higher costs of living.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: On this basis, I reflected on the GST implementation and design.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: A simplistic GST system is, by nature, regressive.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
