text: However, factoring the GST Assurance Package and the Permanent GST Voucher scheme that have been in place since 2012, the net effect is one where the impact of the GST increase is different across the different income segments of our population.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: What is salient and is key is that, taken holistically, the support packages transform the GST scheme into a tiered consumption tax system.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It is actually the higher income who will pay closer to the new headline rate of 9%.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: There were suggestions in this House to consider further increasing taxes paid by those in the higher income segment, in place of this proposed GST Bill.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, this proposed GST system, when taken holistically, in fact, taxes those in the higher income significantly more, not only at a higher effective rate, but also because of their relatively higher consumption and, therefore, significantly more spending on luxury goods.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As mentioned, what weighed on my mind was my residents’ and the broader population’s concerns on the GST hike coming at a time of high global inflation, geopolitical tensions and a deteriorating global economic landscape, which all seem like a perfect storm.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Most recently, MOM reported that Singapore’s job market showed signs of slowing momentum, with an uptick in retrenchments.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Amidst rising cost of living, job loss worries will weigh on the minds of residents.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I also welcome the Deputy Prime Minister's announcement today on updating the GST Assurance Package and his continued assurance on further updates to account for further hikes in expected inflation when it happens.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Shifting to the focus on businesses, I understand through the Association of Trade and Commerce the concerns expressed by smaller SMEs.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In particular, those who are non-GST-registered cannot claim GST expenses paid to GST-registered suppliers.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Some considered voluntary GST registration but find it difficult to comply with the requirements due to limited resources.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In the longer term, should economic uncertainties persist and result in lower tax receipts even after the GST increase, can the Deputy Prime Minister share what are other potential levers to ensure we can keep up with our long-term expenditure needs?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government assure us that the GST rate will not increase beyond 9% in the near term?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, as our society spends more and more, it is necessary to raise the GST.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, with inflation and cost of living rising, I am worried that residents will not be able to bear the cost.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, I have examined our GST system very carefully.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I believe that Singapore's GST system, with its unique design, is more in depth and layered.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It can help to address the challenges faced by Singapore in a more practical manner while taking care of the needs of Singaporeans at the same time.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Nevertheless, to Singaporeans, the burden of the cost of living is already very heavy now.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I can understand their concerns about raising GST at this juncture.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I am very glad that the Government has done its part to help Singaporeans when it is needed as they have promised to do so.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that the Deputy Prime Minister will provide more details so that residents can have a greater peace of mind and that Singaporeans will know that the Government will continue to do its utmost to help them, especially those who need help most.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, I hope that the Government can further help local SMEs.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Some small business operators will also face pressures because of the increase in GST as their costs will go up.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, they are also worried that if they raise their prices, they will be seen as profiteering and that their old customers will not accept the new prices.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I believe that the Government will not forget our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: (In English): Sir, in conclusion, I support this GST Bill because of the holistic nature of how it is being executed.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While I have some queries, I am also glad that the Government has tabled this Bill to discuss openly this inconvenient truth about funding for Singapore’s future.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It is an easy thing to speak about spending more but a lot harder to find the means to fund the spend.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: At the heart of the GST Bill is the broader theme about caring for our people, for not just the short but also, importantly, to fund the long-term needs of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Taken in totality, the GST system, with targeted support packages, is part of an inclusive and resilient fiscal structure.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It funds our expenditures while providing support for the lower- and middle-income segment at the same time.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The challenges ahead require us to make this difficult but responsible decision to secure the well-being of all Singaporeans for the longer term.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, just now, Mr Leong quoted a story that was told by former Member of Parliament Lee Bee Wah, and wrote his own version of the story.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And I want to offer some constructive suggestions to Mr Leong so that the next time he tells this story, it can be more accurate and more complete.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We know that in Singapore society, it is more accurate to say that the money Ah Seng gives to Ah Gong is less than the money Ah Gong gives to Ah Seng.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, Ah Gong actually gives more to Ah Seng compared to what Ah Seng gives to Ah Gong.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Thirdly, Mr Leong mentioned that Ah Ma is already old.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Healthcare costs have increased, and Ah Ma needs someone to take care of her.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I feel that Ah Gong and Ah Ma have worked so hard to take care of Ah Seng and bring him up, now that Ah Gong and Ah Ma have aged, it is time that Ah Seng takes care of them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is the right way as filial piety is a virtue in Asian societies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For Ah Gong, he has been very understanding of the difficulties that Ah Seng is facing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: He does not ask Ah Seng to pay for these extra expenses immediately.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Instead, he gave Ah Seng a buffer of five years or even 10 years to help him tide through the challenges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Not for themselves, but for Ah Seng and his children and their future generations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, if Ah Seng asks Ah Gong, why are you saving so much money?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I think Ah Gong may tell him, it is like what the Hokkien song says, "this is all for you".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is because the principal issue that arises for consideration in this Bill, that is, the GST hike, has already been discussed not just during this year's annual Budget debate, but in the speeches made since 2018, after the Government's decision to increase GST was announced.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This long foreshadowing has already led to the Workers' Party (WP) deciding to vote against the GST increase.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It does not cut well because there are, in fact, points of consensus between hon Members of the PAP and WP on several important things.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As stated by my Parliamentary colleague, Mr Liang Eng Hwa, broadly, both parties agreed to higher levels of social spending for the future and acknowledged the need to raise revenue to meet the expenditure; especially against the spectre of an economy that is likely to grow more slowly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Where we come apart, clearly, is whether GST should, and can be, a source of revenue.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And, in this, we appearing to be arguing from exact opposite sides of each other.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, how is it that two parties, which are aligned on all the main objectives, can be so far apart in the assessment of whether or not a GST hike is the proper thing to do for our people?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In 1993, the GST Bill was introduced in this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Then, as now, it was an unpopular move.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Then, as now, there were good reasons to do so – we needed to strengthen our tax base to ensure that our tax structure was resilient and promote enterprise and growth.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In 1993, direct taxes made up about 60% of our tax revenue, of which 73% was income and corporate tax.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Introducing a consumption tax would keep Singapore competitive and also allow us a stable and diversified stream of tax revenues and allow us to invest more heavily in growth.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The WP raised strenuous objections to its passing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member then, Mr Low Thia Khiang, in his speech, felt that there was no basis to suggest that high income and corporate taxes had the effect of driving talent and entrepreneurism away.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He was concerned about the regressive nature of the tax, especially on low-income people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The PAP's response was to recognise the possible shortcomings and work in policy fixes, such as GST offsets for low-income households.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: GST was introduced on 1 April 1994 and what happened thereafter?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, the majority of Singaporeans do not pay income tax.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the meantime, our Government grew our economy by leaps and bounds.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We attracted investments and talent, we had Government transfers to our people, median salaries increased.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In other words, whatever the hon Ministers then, Dr Richard Hu and Mr S Dhanabalan, said on behalf of the Government on that occasion in 1993 would happen, happened.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our tax rates went down, our tax revenues did not.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our social spending went up – benefiting the poorest amongst us the most.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The doomsday prediction that the poor and the lower-income people would be left behind did not materialise.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the issue of timing, it should be borne in mind that, in 1993, there were strong economic growth and budgetary surpluses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It could have been argued that there was no pressing need to pass the GST Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But when you cast your eyes into the long-term, your perspective changes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In 1993, when our economy was strong and our people were young, it was already felt that GST was needed for the long term.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Today, when we are older and the economy is struggling, it turns out that our 1993 decision was correct.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Then, we were recovering from the Asian Financial Crisis of 1997 and the recession in 2001.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our fiscal situation was very tight, the Singapore economy was struggling, revenue needed to be increased to fund expenses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Then, like now, some voices had suggested to defer, but that will heighten the risk of leaving the Government with insufficient funds for healthcare, education and defence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore would then be in a structural deficit.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In a small open economy, this would have had serious consequences for our exchange rate, for the stability of the Singapore dollar.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If we continually run a deficit, the Singapore dollar would go down, inflation up and everything in Singapore, including our CPF savings, would be worthless.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Therefore, we decided to do the difficult thing and proceed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang argued for the increase of the Net Investment Income (NII) ceiling, not unlike what the WP is asking for now.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He also suggested an increase in property tax and sin taxes, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He was, again, concerned about the impact of GST on inflation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong, as he then was, explained why we were unable to avoid a GST hike, much like how Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong explained during the Budget debate this year.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Budget, which included raising of the GST, also contained the new thinking of the Economic Review Committee (ERC), which brought about fundamental changes to our economic policies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It aimed to develop a vibrant sector driven by entrepreneurial energies, fuelled by regional and global competition, all seeking the best return on their ideas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It aimed to attract more global talent, even as we improved and nurtured our own people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It wanted to make our economy more resilient and dynamic through investing in human capital.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But one thing remained the same as in 1993 – the Government saw its role as creating a pro-business, stable environment for the market to operate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Part of this requires the implementation of sound fiscal and monetary policies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At that point, there, too, were questions about the need to reduce direct taxes, the landscape was even more competitive.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He announced the decision to tweak the NII, which was something Mr Low Thia Khiang advocated, to what it is today.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang and Ms Sylvia Lim argued against the GST hike and suggested instead that the Government use even more NII, get revenue from land sales, corporate tax, stamp duties and so on, much like what is being sought today.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He pointed out that it was dangerous to rely on sentiment-driven transactions for Budget purposes and he said, and I quote: "We have no idea whether these improvements would be sustainable and it would be very poor fiscal policy to commit to future expenditure in the hope that short-term spikes in revenue would be sustained" – exactly as what Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said this year.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When Mr Low Thia Khiang and Ms Sylvia Lim suggested that GST should only be considered after we have run out of revenue streams, Senior Minister Tharman stated, and I quote: "This is not the way a responsible Government conducts its fiscal policies".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As hon Member Ms Jessica Tan just said, it is dangerous for the Government to start scrambling to plug revenue gaps when there is an urgent need to do so.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We had a recession in 2008 due to the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Core inflation, at its highest, was at 6.5%.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But we powered through with the GST hike and helped Singaporeans affected by inflation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We focused on creating a more inclusive Singapore with heavy investments in our people, especially the vulnerable, with programmes, such as KidStart, WIS, Silver Support Schemes and so on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This hardwired the GST to a larger redistributive regime and it is fair and progressive.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Today, our economic landscape has been transformed through ITMs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We achieved a remarkable rise in GDP per capita with a larger private sector and a high-value workforce.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But more importantly, quoting Senior Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam in his speech delivered on 14 August 2015 to the Economic Society of Singapore, he said, and I quote: "We achieved broad-based social upliftment, jobs for all, rising incomes for all, homes for all, quality schools and public healthcare for all, and neighbourhoods and parks shared by all".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is not my intention to create a rosy picture of the past.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But by and large, the doomsday predictions of the poor becoming poorer owing to GST hikes simply did not happen.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Returning to 2022, actually, set against the historical context, there is nothing significantly new in what the WP has suggested for this House's consideration.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This leads me to a paragraph in the Hammer article co-written by the hon Members Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Mr Leon Perera entitled "Why the GST Hike is Not Necessary" that was published on 1 July 2022.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They said, and I quote: "Political courage means recognising that the facts and assumptions that supported an earlier decision have changed...

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Political courage means being able to recognise that contrary arguments have merit, even though those arguments come from one's political opponents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Political courage means not opposing for the sake of opposing." I have no trouble with the statements, but, surely, this applies both ways.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: History reveals that the WP has always been taking a conscientious objection to GST, regardless of the effects it has brought about.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim quoted about the Japanese experience of over 25 years to justify his proposition that GST will lead to runaway inflation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I thought it was noteworthy that he did not analyse the Singapore experience instead.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Political courage commands a price, but mere talk of political courage is cheap.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now come the crux of my decision.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Objectively, what has happened in history favoured the PAP.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What we are doing now, as a matter of approach, is no different.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is not just theory; it is almost 30 years of practice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is clear to me that we will continue to have fiscal pressures.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We will have to deal with it, failing which, we will pay a serious price.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We also need to get the balance right, so as not to affect our attraction as a hub for talent and investments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We just increased our personal income tax, property tax and vehicle tax.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To be fair, this was something that the Workers' Party has broadly advocated for.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also support the judgement call at this point not to deplete income from reserves through land sales and increasing the NIRC ceiling.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is asked how much is enough when it comes to our reserves.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And I join Mr Sitoh Yih Pin in expressing his view on the same matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I remember this question came up in the last session of Parliament and I ventured to suggest – think of the Indian Ocean tsunami.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Nobody expected it to happen, but it happened, and we had to deal with it.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There could be a collapse of an Antartica ice shelf and we will have to deal with the ramifications of it.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We may have to accelerate the poder construction.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The point is – no one knows – and if somebody says he knows, he is probably a snake oil salesman.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Tilting it in favour of current needs is, I think, selling our children too short.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In building the Singapore of today, our founding fathers carried us on their shoulders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Through sheer grit and determination, they persevered even though at times, their knees were buckling and they could have easily given up.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We should do the same thing for our children.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is not to say current needs are unimportant.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Government is on record to say that no one will be left behind.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This twin approach must carry on at the same time – fiscal responsibility with inclusivity.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To argue that Government should sequence its actions is to ignore the reality that our Government has to just develop the tentacles to deal with all the multiple existential issues happening at the same time to steer our country out of stormy waters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The answer lies partly in political principle and partly in a difference of political judgement.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On political principle, we part ways on many counts, but just on the point of political courage, the WP sees it as courageous for the PAP to accept good ideas from the WP.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The PAP has pledged to do our best for Singaporeans and being in a small country, we must not care about the pedigree of ideas, merely about their quality.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Hansard is replete with illustrations where suggestions made across the aisle were accepted by the Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We are not so naive as to think that the GST will gain us political favour.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We know that it will be a tough pill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But yet, we still ask this of the Singaporean people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We ask this because there are hard, immovable economic and fiscal realities in public life that can be either sugarcoated beyond recognition or presented in their true form.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The PAP's choice, from 1993 till 2022, has always been the latter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We do so as a matter of principle and also because of our deep and abiding faith in the Singaporean people to understand the need for these hard choices and why we have to make them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is not mere theoretical conviction, but a judgement call born of years of experience in running the government and understanding the global marketplace.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We ask this at this difficult time because we truly believe that it will give us a fairer and more progressive way of financing our government and build a stronger foundation for our nation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The first relates to the technical and operational aspects of the GST regime – I think not so many people spoke about that – but the other set of questions relates to the GST increase itself, which many more Members spoke about.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Derrick Goh suggested that we do more to help small businesses register for GST voluntarily.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I completely agree and we will do more.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will continue to help businesses who wish to register for GST to do so.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will do more to engage SMEs on this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the GST transitional rules, Mr Saktiandi Supaat was concerned that smaller businesses might find it difficult to understand these rules.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have been very mindful of their needs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why since early this year, IRAS has been helping businesses prepare for the GST rate change by conducting monthly live webinars, publishing e-tax guides and FAQs on its website, as well as launching a YouTube video.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Businesses that require more clarifications on the transitional rules can approach IRAS for more assistance.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat also asked how offenders will be prosecuted differently under the new Missing Trader Fraud section 62C.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Providing for this under the GST Act will also empower IRAS to investigate and prosecute these offences more effectively.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As Mr Louis Ng highlighted, there is a clear distinction in the penalties between tiers one and two.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The distinction between tiers is based on the presence of criminal intent.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Where a person knows or has reasonable grounds to believe that his participation is for a fraudulent purpose, he will be prosecuted under tier one, regardless of whether he has full oversight of the entire operation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Where there is no such criminal intent, and yet a person's business entity is eventually used in a specified arrangement, he will face the lesser, strict liability charge under tier two.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This will apply when business owners do not exercise the reasonable care and due diligence expected of them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Establishing criminal intent, like for all criminal offences, is a question of fact that will need to be proven in Court.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The eventual sentencing of cases will be determined by the Courts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: IRAS has provided guidance on its website and through an e-tax guide on how businesses can avoid being drawn into a Missing Trader Fraud arrangement.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Whistle-blowers who report such fraud to IRAS may also receive rewards under IRAS' whistle-blower programme if conditions are met.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These are the technical and operational issues, which I hope I have clarified.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next, let me move on to the questions on the GST rate increase itself.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Members – from the speeches I have heard – broadly agreed that our structural needs are rising and we do need to raise the revenues to fund them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The key issues are how we go about doing so and these issues can be summarised into two broad questions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, why raise the GST now; and second, why not alternatives to the GST?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I fully understand and appreciate Members' concerns about doing so in such a challenging economic environment.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This was a very difficult decision for me and the MOF team.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We had considered this very carefully, leading up to the Budget, as I explained in the Budget speech and in our Budget debate and subsequently, even after the Budget when we saw conditions deteriorating.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But eventually, we decided that it was still necessary to move.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For now, our economy and labour market are still holding steady.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Our GDP growth is projected to come in at 3% to 4% this year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Our resident unemployment rate has also recovered to pre-pandemic levels.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Sectors such as aviation and tourism that were badly affected by the pandemic are continuing to recover.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are some indications of weaker growth in some sectors and we are monitoring this closely.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: More importantly, the economic challenges we face are not just near-term or cyclical in nature.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The ongoing war in Ukraine, disruptions to energy and food supplies as well as rising geopolitical tensions and more fragmented supply chains – these are the realities that we have to deal with not just in the near-term but very possibly for a more prolonged period.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In other words, international economic conditions have fundamentally changed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: While we expect inflationary pressures in Singapore to ease in the second half of next year, according to MAS' latest forecast, inflation rates are unlikely to go back to what they were over the past decade.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If you take the example of a middle-income family – which I think Mr Louis Chua highlighted just now in his speech – inflation is coming in at 6% this year, their annual expenditure will go up by – Mr Louis Chua estimated – around $2.700.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, yes, there is an increase in spending because of inflation, but the support they are getting this year is around $1,500.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it will, again, keep to our commitment to offset more than half of the inflation-driven increase in cost of living this year for middle-income households.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This does not take into account wage increases for individuals, which many of whom are very likely to enjoy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is what we are doing this year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next year, we will continue to monitor closely the inflation situation and we will assess what additional support measures might be needed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At the same time, we will press ahead with our economic restructuring and transformation plans because when we make ourselves more productive and competitive, our workers will be able to earn more and this can more than make up for the higher prices and ensure that we are better off in real terms.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked if the GST rate increase is the right macroeconomic stance to adopt in the face of higher inflation and a slowing economy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have designed our assistance packages to start flowing support early, ahead of the GST rate increase.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As a result, the combined impact of the GST increase and the offset schemes we have put in place is broadly fiscally neutral.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Furthermore, we are targeting our support at the lower- to middle-income households rather than doing it in a broad-based manner.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In sum, we have designed the overall package to ensure we neither stoke inflation inadvertently nor choke aggregate demand.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is an appropriate macroeconomic stance to adopt at this juncture.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim cited what happened in Japan when they increased the GST rate as a warning of what might happen.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But surely as a professional economist, Assoc Prof Lim must know better.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They raised GST and their inflation doubled, yes, but from a chronically low 1% to 2% and, even then, temporarily.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, let us avoid raising these alarmist examples that may not be so relevant to our context.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Does that mean there is nothing to learn from overseas?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: No, we must continue to learn from countries' experience, but let us make sure we get the right lessons.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, there are no end of international examples, including recent ones, where governments have weakened their foundations of their fiscal systems and they have ended up paying a very major price.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, let us never, ever be tempted to go down that route.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: While there are considerable uncertainties in the economic outlook, there is certainly nothing uncertain about Government expenditures, especially in the area of healthcare, which many Members have cited, including Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Mr Sharael Taha and Ms Joan Pereira.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Our population is ageing with every passing year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is 1.3 percentage points of GDP, much more than the revenues we get from the GST increase.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, even as we deal with healthcare spending, we have to resource many other spending needs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, we want to invest more in early childhood education, to give every child the best start in life.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Annual spending there is expected to double to over $2 billion in the next few years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We also want to do more to uplift our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Surely, there is unanimous agreement in this House to do more here.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will continue to closely monitor the progress of our efforts to uplift the wages of lower-wage workers and we stand ready to do more if needed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling also highlighted concerns about SMEs and self-employed persons and we are also looking at how we can do more to help them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Today, public housing is a key concern for many and we are ramping up our BTO supply to ensure accessibility and affordability of public housing and to address the backlogs due to COVID-19 amid higher construction costs, and all that will, again, cost more.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We also need to spend more to strengthen our social compact.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is an exercise we are undertaking now through the Forward Singapore conversations, and we are considering further policy shifts to do more for disadvantaged and vulnerable groups.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, healthcare already, you can see where the spending needs are going to be, it is very clear, because of the ageing population.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Then, you add up all of these other needs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is a few billion here and a few billion there – they all add up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: None of these needs have become less urgent because of the global economic situation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the contrary, we must do more, especially in an uncertain and volatile environment.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But what we can and what we will do is to delay the impact of the GST increase.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is done through the Assurance Package for the majority of Singaporean households for at least five years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In the meantime, as Members noted, we can then start to benefit from the recovery in tourism and collect more GST from tourists, foreigners and those who are better-off.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is the reason why we are doing it like that, because people say, forget your Assurance Package.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I do not do the Assurance Package, do not do GST, we square off and we will just do GST later.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But do not forget, when we do it the way we have designed, revenues start flowing in.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: From foreigners, from the better off people, from tourists.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we are already getting benefits from revenue sources from these groups through the way we have designed the system.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat also asked whether we would proceed with the second step of the GST rate increase if there were a sharp deterioration in the economic conditions next year, like a major global downturn.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For now, this is not our baseline expectation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next, let me talk on the second set of questions around why not consider alternatives to the GST?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim and Mr Louis Chua suggested that there was fiscal surplus or fiscal slack, which would enable us to delay the GST.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I wish that were so, but unfortunately, we do not have any surplus.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim said that the Government is shielded from inflation because when inflation goes up and prices are higher, we will automatically collect more revenues in nominal terms.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But do not forget, and he did not mention this, Government spending must also go up correspondingly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Are we going to deny them wage increases?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Support schemes must go up surely, to keep pace with inflation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, on both sides, yes, we may collect more in nominal terms, but we will also have to spend more.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we have already used this surplus, as well as the better-than-expected fiscal outturn for the first half of FY2022 to fund the June and October support packages this year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At this stage, it is still too early to determine the eventual fiscal outturn for the second half of FY2022.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But for now, we are not expecting a surplus for the year and we will provide a firmer update, of course, at next year's Budget.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But the bottom line is, any surpluses that you can think of are imaginary.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They are not there and will not allow us to delay the GST.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The second set of suggestions of alternatives are largely to use more from the past reserves.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And there, you have different variants, including tweaking the formula for NIRC from 50% to 60% or changing the definition of land sales revenues so that all the revenue from land sold attributable to the first 10 years of lease goes into current reserves as opposed to past reserves.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Basically, whichever the suggestion, the point is, these suggestions are asking the Government to use more from the past reserves.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Workers' Party have said that what they are suggesting is not to raid the past reserves, but it is really just to slow down the accumulation in reserves.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It sounds very attractive, but it essentially means that we are leaving our next generation with fewer resources.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This will just make it harder for them to meet future needs at a time when things are going to be more challenging, as Ms Foo Mee Har and many others have highlighted.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At a time when our economy will be maturing, our population will be ageing rapidly and the uncertainties in the world are only becoming greater and greater.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Surely, this cannot be the responsible thing to do.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, let us not succumb to the temptation of taking this easy way out and making things worse for our children and grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In any case, as Mr Derrick Goh has highlighted, the growth of the reserves is already expected to slow, given the significant headwinds in the global investment environment, long-term structural changes that we can see happening in the world, including the rise in geopolitical tensions, climate change, ageing populations, lower productivity growth.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Geopolitical tensions, in particular, might not only reduce investment returns but could even result in conflict or war, which can impact the value of our investments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Derrick Goh had asked about the process to determine the long-term expected real rate of return, given these structural trends, and I assure him that we have a robust process in place.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Basically, before the start of each financial year, the investment entities – MAS, GIC and Temasek – will calculate the expected long-term real rate of return for the assets they each manage.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This has to be certified by their respective boards and then they will submit it to the Government.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Government would take these inputs to propose the overall long-term expected real rate of return to the President.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The President will consult with the Council of Presidential Advisors before deciding whether to agree with the Government's proposal.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it is a very robust system with a few layers of checks in place.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that is the second broad range of suggestions – to use more from the past reserves.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I heard just now from Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, the third area of suggestion which is to fine-tune the GST system to have exemptions for essentials.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is something that Ms He Ting Ru had suggested during the Budget debate as well and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim has reiterated that proposal.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is, again, one of those things that sounds like a wonderful idea.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But the road to perdition is paved with many good intentions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And this is not just from our analysis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: You look around the world, multi-tier GST systems have lots of problems, huge difficulties trying to distinguish between the products.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The system is so costly, it is onerous to implement and it becomes very, very cumbersome.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: More recently, I saw a BBC article about the Indian system.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Pizza toppings are now deemed not to be classified as cheese.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: A fifth of the toppings are made by vegetable oil and vegetable oil is not considered cheese.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, they charge GST at a higher rate of 18% for what they deem as "edible preparations" rather than at 12%, which is the rate for cheese.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And this had to go through the Courts and it was determined by the Courts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is what we have seen everywhere and the bigger problem behind this is just that besides the administration, the cumbersomeness, the complication, it is just not effective.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It sounds good on paper but it is not effective because when you exempt a basket of goods like essential items, in the end, you benefit the well-to-do because the well-to-do will spend more on everything, not just luxury items, but basic necessities as well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And this is a conclusion not just made by us.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is a conclusion reached by studies, based on studies by numerous governments as well as organisations like the OECD.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we have more than enough evidence to show that this multi-tier system does not work effectively.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, let us not try to come up with ideas that sound good on paper, sound attractive, but in the end, we know, not just because we do not like the idea, not just because we are not open to new ideas, but we know from independent analyses done by other countries, done by the OECD, that these ideas, these alternatives, do not work.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, we have designed a different system in Singapore, which is, as I described in my first speech just now, also multi-tier, but it is multi-tiered by income and it is a far more effective system.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim said it was a patchwork of offsets.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Well, I think he does not give Singapore enough credit.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If you look around the world at any GST system, I dare say we are one of the few, if not the only country with such an effective system of GST that has taxed consumption fairly and effectively.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Certainly, not a patchwork, but a thorough, deliberate design of the GST system to make it fair and effective.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The fourth idea to why not alternatives to GST is, let us look at other revenue alternatives.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Whether it is property tax, personal income tax, corporate income tax.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Let us look at all these other revenue alternatives.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We went through them in great detail at the Budget debate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The problem with these ideas, not because we are not open to them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have considered all of them carefully and, in fact, in the Budget, we did raise property tax, we did raise personal income tax as well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But the problem with these ideas, as a substitute for the GST, is that simply the sums do not add up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Property tax on residential property yields only $1 billion in annual revenue, today.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: How much more do you want to get from property tax?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have already raised it significantly this Budget for the high-end properties.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: You want to get more revenues from property tax, you will inevitably have to cover a wider group of property owners, including the middle-income.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Why would the top earners stay in Singapore and pay 42% tax?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, again, inevitably when you talk about personal income tax, any way to get more revenue, will inevitably mean higher rates for a broader group of income earners.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Yes, there is BEPS 2.0 which may yield more revenue, according to some estimates .

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But it is really too early to determine how much we will get from the changes in BEPS 2.0 because as I keep saying, there are two pillars in BEPS 2.0 – Pillar One, Pillar Two.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We may get some revenue there, but we have to look at the combined effects of Pillars One and Two.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And even after looking at all that, even if we do get additional revenues, the reality is that global competition for investments will only get more intense in this new environment.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: With geopolitical tensions going up, countries are talking about reshoring, friend-shoring, onshoring.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: What does that mean? "Investments come back to my country." And governments are offering very generous subsidies and grants to attract these investments back.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Never mind BEPS 2.0 and corporate minimum tax rates of 15%.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They are offering very attractive packages to attract these investments back to their home countries.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, I have gone through these four different buckets of ideas: fiscal surpluses, use more from past reserves, zero-rating, multi-tiered GST, tap on other revenue alternatives.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And I have explained why actually it is very hard to for any of them to replace the GST increase.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have not talked about lower-wage workers, early childhood, all the other meritorious things we want to do.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, really, the question is not GST or these other alternatives.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why from MOF's point of view, we will continue to study all other fiscal options, all other revenue options and consider how best over time to ensure more resilient and more sustainable revenues for the future.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Having explained my position and also gone through all these different alternative ideas, I should say one thing, which is, I also take issue with the way that Opposition Members and especially Members of the Workers' Party have characterised the Government's position.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Essentially, they have painted a very simplistic narrative.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That Government has not considered these alternatives, that we are on autopilot, we are not open to ideas, we are just stubbornly pushing away at something we decided to do anyway.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is completely false because we have gone through this already in the Budget debate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I have explained repeatedly in the Budget debate that we had thought about all the options very carefully, explained why many of these alternatives are not substitutes for GST.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, I have said it is not just GST or these alternatives.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have to consider so many different options together given our huge funding gap and I have also explained that we have studied this carefully before we made the decision, the very difficult decision to proceed, both in the Budget and after the Budget.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, this false and simplistic narrative painted by the Workers' Party which, as Mr Murali Pillai has kindly reminded us, is not the first time.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: A pattern of repeating the same arguments against the GST, time and again.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Really, it does not do justice to the commitment and professionalism of the entire team in MOF, including the public officials who are trying so hard to do what is right and to pursue a strategy of fiscal responsibility and discipline for the benefit of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: To be clear, the Workers' Party is entitled to your own position.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: By all means oppose the GST, adopt a different position.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But at least be honest and responsible – acknowledge that your alternatives will either end up requiring the middle-income to pay more or will use more of the past reserves therefore, less for the next generation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And at least have the decency to acknowledge that the Government had considered all of these alternatives carefully.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We debated them in the Budget – thoroughly and rigorously – before we decided on this move.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I would have thought that is what a responsible political party would have done.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Unfortunately, I am very disappointed that the Workers' Party has chosen to take a different path.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There were many Members who had supported the increase in GST but had suggested ways to fine-tune our support schemes and I have listened to many of your suggestions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Ms Jessica Tan asked about the qualifying criteria and administration of the GSTV scheme.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I assure them that we will review the qualifying criteria from time to time to ensure they stay relevant.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Ms Jessica Tan also highlighted a situation where individuals in genuine need miss out on the benefits due to the Annual Value of the property they live in.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And as we have explained, aside from the regular reviews which we do, such individuals may write in, and we will consider appeals on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Ms Foo Mee Har and Ms Joan Pereira suggested making it easier for people to understand our schemes and how they can benefit.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Those who are not sure of their eligibility may refer to the GSTV website, as well as MOF’s website and the various press releases that we put out for more information.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will certainly continue to review to see how we can make information more easily accessible to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I want to also assure Members that we keep a close eye on improving the administration of the GSTV scheme.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Quite a number of Members had shared concerns about businesses profiteering from the GST rate increase and they raised the need for an effective deterrence.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Committee Against Profiteering (CAP), chaired by Minister of State Low Yen Ling, takes a serious view of unjustified price increases using the GST increase as an excuse.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it actively monitors and reviews all feedback on such cases.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They followed up swiftly and found that there were in fact legitimate reasons for the price increases, such as higher cost of raw materials.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The businesses involved have committed to be transparent in their pricing and communications with consumers, and so far, there have not been any repeat complaints.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Workers' Party and the PSP’s stance is "anything but the GST".

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But the question is also to be asked "why not the GST", especially the GST in the way we have designed it in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Leader, would you like to move on the time limit on speeches?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I can fully understand the concerns such a move will have on lower-income households.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But, again, this is not how we have implemented GST in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I have already explained how after putting together the permanent GST Voucher scheme and GST absorption, we have an overall GST system that taxes consumption in a fair and effective manner.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Government, effectively, pays the additional GST on their behalf during this period.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: A consumption tax, yes, it is regressive if implemented as a standalone measure.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But this is not how we have done it in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have worked hard to design a system where GST is implemented together with permanent offsets through the GST Vouchers to negate that disproportionate impact on lower-income households.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have also taken great pains to make sure that the middle-income households are looked after so that they only pay slightly more GST, but the full impact of the GST, the full burden, is borne largely by high-income households as well as foreigners based here and tourists.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is how we get the benefits of the GST system, which is a broad-based consumption tax without its drawbacks.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: What we have is a much, much better alternative than taking more from future generations or significantly raising property or personal income taxes on the broad middle class.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is, certainly, a more responsible approach than planning on the basis of revenues or surpluses that may not materialise.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The unique way we have implemented GST in Singapore reflects the ethos of this Government and the way we have always worked.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We do not just go for politically expedient measures that may very well end up being unviable or unsustainable.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Instead, we focus our efforts on designing effective policies to benefit all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This may mean that the policies are a little bit more complicated.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It may mean that we have to work harder to explain our schemes, but it is well worth the extra effort to get it right and do the right thing for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: (In Mandarin):   Singapore is a rapidly ageing society and for our future healthcare and other needs, we need to raise the Goods and Services Tax (GST) rate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Government will raise GST in a fair manner and help all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This means that while the GST rate will be raised next year and the year after, most households will only start paying more GST from around 2030.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Besides the Assurance Package, lower- and middle-income households can also receive permanent benefits from the GSTV scheme.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At the same time, the Government will continue to absorb GST for publicly-subsidised healthcare and education.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Through these ways, lower-income households pay a much lower effective GST rate than higher-income households.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This includes many retiree households with no income.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Even with an increase in the GST rate, lower-income families will not be affected.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Singapore has implemented the GST in a unique way, taking care of lower- and middle-income households.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I am deeply grateful for the strong trust between the Government and people.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Over the years, this has enabled us to implement many policies to improve the lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I assure everyone that the Government will uphold our principles and values and continue to do the right thing for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Let us uphold this trust in one another and chart our way forward together.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: (In English): Sir, the interests of Singaporeans are at the centre of everything we do.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: No government, no finance minister likes to talk about raising taxes, certainly not a tax like GST.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But if we have to raise taxes, we will always be honest, transparent and we will do so in a fair manner and we will always be accountable to Singaporeans that the resources will be put to good use for their benefit.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I am deeply grateful for the strong compact and trust between the Government and the people.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Over the years, this has allowed us to develop and implement policies to improve the lives for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Singaporeans have benefited from inclusive growth, particularly through our moves to uplift lower-wage workers' incomes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Income inequality in Singapore has been on a steady downtrend.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have strengthened social security through schemes like Silver Support.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have strengthened healthcare assurance for all by building five new polyclinics and doubling the number of community hospital beds in the last decade.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In times of need, such as during the pandemic and during the period of high inflation this year, we have stepped in decisively with measures to support Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Now, as part of Forward Singapore, we are now working in partnership with Singaporeans to refresh and update our social compact for the next bound.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These are but some examples of how we have progressed together as one people and as a nation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, to all Singaporeans, I say you have my assurance that this Government will never compromise on our principles and our values, and we will always do what is right for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Let us keep this trust in each other going as we chart our way forward together.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: If I can have three very short supplementary questions, please.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: The first is with regard to this year's fiscal outturn.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I think the Deputy Prime Minister shared that we do not have any surplus this year but, at the same time, it is too early to determine.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: But also, at the same time, whatever surplus we have is imaginary.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: But as I shared in my speech, just based on the first six months of the operating revenues that have been disclosed so far, we have a $5.8 billion increase in revenue, compared to the year before.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: So, even if we less off the $1.5 billion package in October and $1.4 billion announced today, would it be wrong to say that there is still some slack, at least based on what is disclosed so far?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Second, in terms of the NIRC contribution, is it wrong to say that increasing the NIRC contribution rate will not result in a decline in revenue?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I think an example would be, as I shared in my Budget speech this year, where even if we put into context the drawdown of $43 billion in our reserves for the COVID-19 packages, our reserves today are still higher than they were five years ago.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Lastly, on GST exemption and all that, at this point in time, based on my understanding, there are already provisions of zero-rated GST for exports of goods and international services.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: At the same time, there are certain classes of goods and services that are exempted from GST, such as the sale of residential properties and the provision of financial services as well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: He has not looked at the spending side, which I mentioned just now.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Yes, revenues have gone up in the first half of fiscal year 2022 but spending has gone up as well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: What happens in the second half of FY2022 is still to be seen.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we will, at the end, in the Budget next year, give a firmer estimate, as we always do.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we will continue to monitor and update where necessary.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On GST exemption, yes, there are certain classes of items which are exempt or zero-rated today but they are done for very good reasons, including difficulties in collection and we have kept it to a very, very, very tiny group of items.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Look around at all the GST systems in the world, I think ours, we have kept it very, very limited.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: By and large, most items are taxed on a single-rate GST and if we were to expand the exemption of zero rate to many more items, for that matter, to essential items, food, then we are talking about a large expansion of exmempting of zero-rating in our GST system.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: All the complications, all the downsides, all the problems, all the ineffectiveness that we have seen in other countries will be experienced in Singapore, too.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The Deputy Prime Minister reiterated that he and his MOF colleagues do not believe that it is possible to delay the hike.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If I could just confirm my first question that the estimates of impending healthcare needs over the next two years are, in fact, so urgent that they cannot be delayed even for the short run such that, in the absence of the hike, the Government will inevitably find itself in a deficit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: My second point is to clarify that I was not, in fact, being alarmist in my speech about potential inflationary consequences of the hike.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In fact, I clearly explained that the Japanese environment was different but since the Deputy Prime Minister is so confident in his claim that there will not be an increase in inflation as a result, I wonder if the Government will, in fact, commit to a pause in GST increases to 9% if inflation does turn out to be higher than expected as a result of the hike.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I think the whole point was that we should use the current circumstances as a way to pilot the idea.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I think we have never shied away from talking about how policies need to work for us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I wonder if he would agree that the postponement of GST on essential items actually affords us this opportunity to testbed this idea.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are delaying for more than five years with the Assurance Package.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, I am not sure why I would want to delay only for one to two years because I can delay for much longer.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And with the design of the scheme that we have done, as I have mentioned just now, delaying for the vast majority of Singaporeans but getting those who can pay to pay first.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I mentioned just now the circumstances under which we might reconsider the second step.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is really in the event of a very significant change in the external environment, globally and then impacting Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This has to do not just with inflation, but with the economy, with labour markets, for example, if we were to go into a deep recession next year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not in our baseline expectations at all, but who can tell in this uncertain world what can unfold?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not as though we are reluctant to take in new ideas and to consider pilot schemes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We always do and we are always open to experimentation and policy reviews, but on this particular case, it is not for lack of studies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There has been considerable amount of work done to look at the effectiveness of multi-tiered systems all over the world by governments, by independent organisations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have looked at all of these studies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And when the studies are overwhelmingly negative, it ought to give us pause to consider, is it even necessary to pursue a pilot for Singapore's circumstances, or should we think of alternative solutions?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is exactly what we have done.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have developed a different system in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Also, a multi-tiered system, but I dare say, a more effective multi-tiered system, because the GST is tiered by income and we ensure that we can tax consumption in a way that is fair and effective.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: First of all, allow me to thank the Minister for a very engaging and useful debate today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Maybe this is the second time we are debating on GST in this Chamber.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Allow me a little bit of preamble, just one minute.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But before that, let me say one thing, is that the basic differences between the position, at least for PSP and the Government, is that we think that the Government still did not appreciate enough the financial position that the Singaporeans are in.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: They are not just paying taxes, there are many kinds of indirect taxes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: As a result, let me quote one thing —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, Mr Leong, please proceed to your clarifications.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It is not an opportunity to repeat your speech again.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Even when we talk about the NIRC, we are trying to fanthom up this whole money scheme, the fiscal system that the Government has on the people.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, let me just talk about the NIRC.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Two questions to Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, please.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We give 50% of the NIR to the Budget, right?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But what is the share of NIRC that is not spent in the Budget year?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Two, there are operating expenditures in the Budget and recently we have discovered, you have HDB grants which cost the Budget money, deficit to the Budget, and this in turn, will eat into the NIRC that you contributed, right?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, I ask you the second question: did the NIRC contributed by the past land sales cover the deficit of the HDB grant?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Every revenue we collect, including through the NIRC, is spent.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Second, on the HDB grant and Mr Leong Mun Wai says, "We have just discovered".

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I am not sure how he just discovered this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And therefore, there is a Government funding to HDB.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This has always been the basis of our system, because we want to assure Singaporeans that they will always be able to afford HDB flats in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I have expected the Deputy Prime Minister to answer like that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: There is a large share of the NIRC being apportioned to funds, right?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Just like a few years back, you took $6 billion out of the NIRC and put it in the GST Voucher.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, that means, for that particular year, I think it was 2018, we do not have $6 billion benefit from NIRC.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, one would think that we have been discussing a lot today – would the Deputy Prime Minister commit that in the future, all NIRC will be spent in the current year?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I asked, the HDB grant, like this year, the grant may be close to $4.5 billion, $4.8 billion to cover the deficit of the HDB.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, the amount of NIRC will be reduced by that amount, right?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because you have to pay for the HDB grant.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And besides that, there are other expenditures, which two of them I have mentioned in my last Adjournment Motion speech.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is not what we do in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: All the revenue sources come in; because monies are fungible, this is a general pot of funding.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And then, we spend according to our priorities and therefore there is no point going through and identifying these sorts of linkages.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the first point of whether or not there will be unspent funding, it is the same point.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Generally, we do not believe that there will be surpluses, because we are running such a tight ship now, these days.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But should it happen, for example, that we have an unexpected windfall, a good year, maybe because of property sentiments, cyclical reasons why revenue has some upside, can it happen?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Maybe, from time to time, it can happen.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Then, what is the right response for us to do?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Do you think we would only need $5 billion for climate change adaptation?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, in a good year, for example, if we have that extra money, we will look at longer-term needs and we will set aside these funds prudently, as we have always done to manage our fiscal and finances in a responsible manner.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I just have a few points of clarification and firstly, I thank the Deputy Prime Minister for his replies and to respond to the hon Member Mr Murali Pillai, I think there are points of agreement between the PAP and the Workers' Party in this debate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We are not advocating going to debt markets, for example, to finance a deficit, to make the constitutional changes necessary to do that, we are not advocating that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, there are points of agreement, but I think the disagreement is philosophic and it has to do principally, I think, with the slope of the reserves growth and we advocate for certain measures that would slow the slope of the reserves growth and PAP disagrees with that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: How large is that as a proportion of the reserves, I am not asking that as a question, I know the Government's position on that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But by most estimates that have been in circulation, it is a very, very small fraction.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, it begs the question, how much is enough?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And we are at this stage as a society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: When we are at this level, this quantitative level of financial reserves.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And given that it was 15 years since the framework was last revised, does the Minister and the Government not acknowledge that it behooves us to work on these options at this point in time?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So that is my first point of clarification.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My second point of clarification is I wonder if the Deputy Prime Minister underestimates the risk of inflation specifically regards to this point.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: When the GST hike comes into effect in January next year, we have all acknowledged that may be an issue of some merchants using that as an excuse to increase prices more than necessary, and this is common everywhere in the world.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We have a Committee Against Profiteering, but I think we should also acknowledge it is very difficult for any Committee in a time when inflation is running at very high levels to sort of effectively address and disentangle legitimate price hikes from profiteering-related price hikes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And in fact, many members of the public may not even raise feedback to the Committee because they may think that if certain prices by certain merchants are going up, well, that is just because of inflation, it is not because of profiteering.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, from a point of view of practical execution, will the Deputy Prime Minister agree that it is very difficult to clamp down on this potential for profiteering and therefore, there is a macroeconomic inflation risk from introducing GST in the calendar year next year.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I take the Deputy Prime Minister's point that fiscally it is neutral but there is this other risk of macroeconomic inflation.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If you can keep the third clarification shorter than the first two.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I did not hear the Deputy Prime Minister responding to my colleague, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim on this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: How much is that going to be increasing in the next few years and does the rate of healthcare expenditure increase in the next few years, the projected rate, does that require urgency about hiking the GST next year or the year after?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is no need to have fancy words. "Slow down the rate of growth of reserves".

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Basically, you are asking to use more of the past reserves and leaving behind less for the next generation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Fine, that is a legitimate position to have, but is this a wise thing to do?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Is it a responsible thing to do, considering the new global environment that we are in, the uncertainties that we face, all the challenges that many Members here have spoken about.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
